1→# ![C++](https://img.shields.io/badge/c++-%2300599C.svg?style=for-the-badge&logo=c%2B%2B&logoColor=white) sqlgen 
     2→
     3→[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
     4→[![Maintenance](https://img.shields.io/badge/Maintained%3F-yes-green.svg)](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp/graphs/commit-activity)
     5→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/C++-20-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     6→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/gcc-11+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     7→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/clang-14+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     8→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/MSVC-17+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     9→
    10→**📖 Documentation**: [Click here](docs/README.md)
    11→
    12→**sqlgen** is a modern, type-safe ORM and SQL query generator for C++20, inspired by Python's [SQLAlchemy](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy)/[SQLModel](https://github.com/fastapi/sqlmodel) and Rust's [Diesel](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel). It provides a fluent, composable interface for database operations with compile-time type checking and SQL injection protection.
    13→
    14→sqlgen is based on and tightly integrated with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp), a C++-20 library for fast serialization, deserialization and validation using reflection, similar to pydantic in Python, serde in Rust, encoding in Go or aeson in Haskell.
    15→
    16→Together, reflect-cpp and sqlgen enable reliable and efficient ETL pipelines.
    17→
    18→## Features
    19→
    20→- 🔒 **Type Safety**: Compile-time validation of table schemas and queries
    21→- 🛡️ **SQL Injection Protection**: Built-in input validation and parameterized queries
    22→- 🔄 **Composable Queries**: Fluent interface for building complex queries
    23→- 🚀 **High Performance**: Efficient batch operations and prepared statements
    24→- 📦 **Modern C++**: Leverages C++20 features for a clean, expressive API
    25→- 🔌 **Multiple Backends**: Support for PostgreSQL and SQLite
    26→- 🔍 **Reflection Integration**: Seamless integration with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp) 
    27→
    28→## Supported databases 
    29→
    30→The following table lists the databases currently supported by sqlgen and the underlying libraries used:
    31→
    32→| Database      | Library                                                                  | Version      | License       | Remarks                                              |
    33→|---------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------|---------------| -----------------------------------------------------|
    34→| MySQL/MariaDB | [libmariadb](https://github.com/mariadb-corporation/mariadb-connector-c) | >= 3.4.5     | LGPL          |                                                      |
    35→| PostgreSQL    | [libpq](https://github.com/postgres/postgres)                            | >= 16.4      | PostgreSQL    | Will work for all libpq-compatible databases         |
    36→| sqlite        | [sqlite](https://sqlite.org/index.html)                                  | >= 3.49.1    | Public Domain |                                                      |
    37→
    38→## Quick Start
    39→
    40→### Installation using vcpkg
    41→
    42→1. Make sure you have the required dependencies installed (skip this step on Windows):
    43→```bash
    44→sudo apt-get install autoconf bison flex # Linux (Ubuntu, Debian, ...)
    45→brew install autoconf bison flex # macOS
    46→```
    47→
    48→2. Set up vcpkg:
    49→```bash
    50→git submodule update --init
    51→./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.sh  # Linux, macOS
    52→./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.bat # Windows
    53→```
    54→
    55→3. Build the library:
    56→```bash
    57→cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_CXX_STANDARD=20 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
    58→cmake --build build -j 4  # gcc, clang
    59→cmake --build build --config Release -j 4  # MSVC
    60→```
    61→
    62→This will build the static library. To build the shared library 
    63→add `-DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON -DVCPKG_TARGET_TRIPLET=...` to the first line.
    64→Run `./vcpkg/vcpkg help triplets` to view all supported triplets. 
    65→Common triplets for shared libraries are `x64-linux-dynamic`, 
    66→`arm64-osx-dynamic` or `x64-osx-dynamic`.   
    67→
    68→Add `-DSQLGEN_MYSQL=ON` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
    69→
    70→4. Include in your CMake project:
    71→```cmake
    72→find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)
    73→target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
    74→```
    75→
    76→### Installation using Conan
    77→
    78→1. Install Conan (assuming you have Python and pipx installed):
    79→
    80→```bash
    81→pipx install conan
    82→conan profile detect
    83→```
    84→
    85→For older versions of pip, you can also use `pip` instead of `pipx`.
    86→
    87→2. Build the library:
    88→
    89→```bash
    90→conan build . --build=missing -s compiler.cppstd=gnu20
    91→```
    92→
    93→This will build the static library. To build the shared library,
    94→add `-o */*:shared=True`. 
    95→
    96→Add `-o sqlgen/*:with_mysql=True` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
    97→
    98→3. Include in your CMake project:
    99→```cmake
   100→find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)
   101→target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
   102→```
   103→
   104→You can call `conan inspect .` to get an overview of the supported options.
   105→
   106→## Usage Examples
   107→
   108→### Hello World
   109→
   110→```cpp
   111→#include <sqlgen/sqlite.hpp>
   112→#include <iostream>
   113→
   114→struct User {
   115→    std::string name;
   116→    int age;
   117→};
   118→
   119→int main() {
   120→    // Connect to SQLite database
   121→    const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("test.db");
   122→    
   123→    // Create and insert a user
   124→    const auto user = User{.name = "John", .age = 30};
   125→    sqlgen::write(conn, user);
   126→    
   127→    // Read all users
   128→    const auto users = sqlgen::read<std::vector<User>>(conn).value();
   129→    
   130→    for (const auto& u : users) {
   131→        std::cout << u.name << " is " << u.age << " years old\n";
   132→    }
   133→}
   134→```
   135→
   136→### Connecting to a Database
   137→
   138→```cpp
   139→#include <sqlgen/postgres.hpp>
   140→
   141→// PostgreSQL connection
   142→const auto credentials = sqlgen::postgres::Credentials{
   143→    .user = "username",
   144→    .password = "password",
   145→    .host = "localhost",
   146→    .dbname = "mydb",
   147→    .port = 5432
   148→};
   149→
   150→const auto conn = sqlgen::postgres::connect(credentials);
   151→
   152→// SQLite connection
   153→const auto sqlite_conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
   154→```
   155→
   156→### Defining Models
   157→
   158→```cpp
   159→struct Person {
   160→    std::string first_name;
   161→    std::string last_name;
   162→    uint32_t age;
   163→    std::optional<std::string> email;  // Nullable field
   164→};
   165→```
   166→
   167→### Inserting Data
   168→
   169→```cpp
   170→const auto people = std::vector<Person>({
   171→    Person{.first_name = "Homer", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 45},
   172→    Person{.first_name = "Marge", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 42}
   173→});
   174→
   175→// Automatically creates table if it doesn't exist
   176→// (recall that the table is fully defined at compile time)
   177→const auto result = sqlgen::write(conn, people);
   178→
   179→if (!result) {
   180→    std::cerr << "Error: " << result.error().what() << std::endl;
   181→}
   182→```
   183→
   184→Or:
   185→
   186→```cpp
   187→...
   188→
   189→// write(...) abstracts these steps away, but
   190→// if you prefer more granular control, you
   191→// can use sqlgen::insert.
   192→const auto result = begin_transaction(conn)
   193→                        .and_then(create_table<Person> | if_not_exists)
   194→                        .and_then(insert(std::ref(people)))
   195→                        .and_then(commit);
   196→
   197→...
   198→```
   199→
   200→Generated SQL:
   201→```sql
   202→BEGIN TRANSACTION;
   203→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Person" (
   204→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
   205→    "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
   206→    "age" INTEGER NOT NULL,
   207→    "email" TEXT
   208→);
   209→
   210→INSERT INTO "Person" ("first_name", "last_name", "age", "email") 
   211→VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?);
   212→COMMIT;
   213→```
   214→
   215→### Querying Data
   216→
   217→```cpp
   218→#include <rfl/json.hpp>
   219→#include <sqlgen/postgres.hpp>
   220→
   221→using namespace sqlgen;
   222→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   223→
   224→// Build a query for adults, ordered by age
   225→const auto query = read<std::vector<Person>> |
   226→                   where("age"_c >= 18) |
   227→                   order_by("age"_c.desc(), "last_name"_c) |
   228→                   limit(10);
   229→
   230→// Execute the query
   231→const auto result = query(conn);
   232→
   233→if (result) {
   234→    // Print results as JSON
   235→    std::cout << rfl::json::write(*result) << std::endl;
   236→} else {
   237→    std::cerr << "Error: " << result.error().what() << std::endl;
   238→}
   239→```
   240→
   241→Generated SQL:
   242→```sql
   243→SELECT "first_name", "last_name", "age", "email"
   244→FROM "Person"
   245→WHERE "age" >= 18
   246→ORDER BY "age" DESC, "last_name"
   247→LIMIT 10;
   248→```
   249→
   250→### Grouping and Aggregating Data
   251→
   252→```cpp
   253→using namespace sqlgen;
   254→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   255→
   256→struct Children {
   257→    std::string last_name;
   258→    int num_children;
   259→    int max_age;
   260→    int min_age;
   261→    int sum_age;
   262→};
   263→
   264→const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
   265→    "last_name"_c,
   266→    count().as<"num_children">(),
   267→    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),
   268→    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),
   269→    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),
   270→) | where("age"_c < 18) | group_by("last_name"_c) | to<std::vector<Children>>;
   271→
   272→const std::vector<Children> children = get_children(conn).value();
   273→```
   274→
   275→Generated SQL:
   276→```sql
   277→SELECT 
   278→    "last_name",
   279→    COUNT(*) as "num_children",
   280→    MAX("age") as "max_age",
   281→    MIN("age") as "min_age",
   282→    SUM("age") as "sum_age"
   283→FROM "Person"

   287→
   288→### Joining data
   289→
   290→```cpp

   292→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   293→
   294→struct ParentAndChild {

   373→) t2 
   374→ON t1."id" = t2."id" 
   375→ORDER BY t1."id", t2."id"
   376→```
   377→
   378→Or:
   379→```cpp
   380→using namespace sqlgen;
   381→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   382→
   383→struct ParentAndChild {
   384→    std::string last_name;
   385→    std::string first_name_parent;
   386→    std::string first_name_child;
   387→    double parent_age_at_birth;
   388→};
   389→
   390→// First, create a subquery
   391→const auto get_parents = select_from<Person, "t1">(
   392→    "child_id"_t2 | as<"id">,
   393→    "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name">,
   394→    "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   395→    "age"_t1 | as<"age">
   396→) | inner_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2);
   397→
   398→// Then use it as a source for another query
   399→const auto get_people = select_from<"t1">(
   400→    get_parents,  // Use the subquery as the source
   401→    "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   402→    "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name_parent">,
   403→    "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
   404→    ("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"parent_age_at_birth">) | 
   405→ inner_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t1 == "id"_t2) | 
   406→ order_by("id"_t1, "id"_t2) | to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   407→```
   408→
   409→Generated SQL:
   410→```sql
   411→SELECT t1."last_name" AS "last_name", 
   412→       t1."first_name" AS "first_name_parent", 
   413→       t2."first_name" AS "first_name_child", 
   414→       (t1."age") - (t2."age") AS "parent_age_at_birth" 
   415→FROM (
   416→    SELECT t2."child_id" AS "id", 
   417→           t1."first_name" AS "first_name", 
   418→           t1."last_name" AS "last_name", 
   419→           t1."age" AS "age" 
   420→    FROM "Person" t1 
   421→    INNER JOIN "Relationship" t2
   422→    ON t1."id" = t2."parent_id"
   423→) t1 
   424→INNER JOIN "Person" t2 
   425→ON t1."id" = t2."id"
   426→ORDER BY t1."id", t2."id"
   427→```
   428→
   429→### Type Safety and SQL Injection Protection
   430→
   431→sqlgen provides comprehensive compile-time checks and runtime protection:
   432→
   433→```cpp
   434→// Compile-time error: No such column "color"
   435→const auto query = read<std::vector<Person>> |
   436→                   where("color"_c == "blue");
   437→
   438→// Compile-time error: Cannot compare column "age" to a string 
   439→const auto query = read<std::vector<Person>> |
   440→                   where("age"_c == "Homer");
   441→
   442→// Compile-time error: "age" must be aggregated or included in GROUP BY 
   443→const auto query = select_from<Person>(
   444→    "last_name"_c,
   445→    "age"_c 
   446→) | group_by("last_name"_c);
   447→
   448→// Compile-time error: Cannot add string and int 
   449→const auto query = select_from<Person>(
   450→    "last_name"_c + "age"_c 
   451→);
   452→
   453→// Runtime protection against SQL injection
   454→std::vector<Person> get_people(const auto& conn, 
   455→                              const sqlgen::AlphaNumeric& first_name) {
   456→    using namespace sqlgen;
   457→    return (read<std::vector<Person>> | 
   458→            where("first_name"_c == first_name))(conn).value();
   459→}
   460→
   461→// This will be rejected
   462→get_people(conn, "Homer' OR '1'='1");  // SQL injection attempt
   463→```

1→# `sqlgen::select_from`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::select_from` function provides a type-safe, composable interface for building SQL SELECT queries in C++. It supports selecting from tables, subqueries, and complex nested queries with full support for joins, filtering, grouping, ordering, and result type conversion.
     4→
     5→## Basic Usage
     6→
     7→### Selecting from a Table
     8→
     9→```cpp
    10→using namespace sqlgen;
    11→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    12→
    13→struct Person {
    14→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id;
    15→    std::string first_name;
    16→    std::string last_name;
    17→    int age;
    18→};
    19→
    20→// Select specific columns
    21→const auto query = select_from<Person>("first_name"_c, "last_name"_c, "age"_c);
    22→
    23→// Execute the query
    24→const auto people = sqlite::connect()
    25→    .and_then(query | to<std::vector<Person>>)
    26→    .value();
    27→```
    28→
    29→This generates:
    30→```sql
    31→SELECT "first_name", "last_name", "age" FROM "Person"
    32→```
    33→
    34→### Selecting with Aliases
    35→
    36→Use aliases to rename columns in the result set:
    37→
    38→```cpp
    39→struct Result {
    40→    std::string name;
    41→    int person_age;
    42→};
    43→
    44→const auto query = select_from<Person>(
    45→    "first_name"_c | as<"name">,
    46→    "age"_c | as<"person_age">
    47→) | to<std::vector<Result>>;
    48→```
    49→
    50→This generates:
    51→```sql
    52→SELECT "first_name" AS "name", "age" AS "person_age" FROM "Person"
    53→```
    54→
    55→## Table Aliases
    56→
    57→### Aliased Tables
    58→
    59→When you need to reference the same table multiple times or want cleaner column references:
    60→
    61→```cpp
    62→const auto query = select_from<Person, "t1">(
    63→    "first_name"_t1,
    64→    "last_name"_t1,
    65→    "age"_t1
    66→) | where("age"_t1 > 18);
    67→```
    68→
    69→This generates:
    70→```sql
    71→SELECT t1."first_name", t1."last_name", t1."age" FROM "Person" t1 WHERE t1."age" > 18
    72→```
    73→
    74→## Selecting from Subqueries
    75→
    76→You can use the result of one query as the source for another query:
    77→
    78→```cpp
    79→// First, create a subquery
    80→const auto get_parents = select_from<Person, "t1">(
    81→    "child_id"_t2 | as<"id">,
    82→    "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name">,
    83→    "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
    84→    "age"_t1 | as<"age">
    85→) | inner_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2);
    86→
    87→// Then use it as a source for another query
    88→const auto get_people = select_from<"t1">(
    89→    get_parents,  // Use the subquery as the source
    90→    "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
    91→    "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name_parent">,
    92→    "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
    93→    ("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"parent_age_at_birth">
    94→) | inner_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t1 == "id"_t2);
    95→```
    96→
    97→This generates:
    98→```sql
    99→SELECT t1."last_name" AS "last_name", t1."first_name" AS "first_name_parent", t2."first_name" AS "first_name_child", (t1."age") - (t2."age") AS "parent_age_at_birth" 
   100→FROM (
   101→    SELECT t2."child_id" AS "id", t1."first_name" AS "first_name", t1."last_name" AS "last_name", t1."age" AS "age" 
   102→    FROM "Person" t1 
   103→    INNER JOIN "Relationship" t2 ON t1."id" = t2."parent_id"
   104→) t1 
   105→INNER JOIN "Person" t2 ON t1."id" = t2."id"
   106→```
   107→
   108→## Expressions and Calculations
   109→
   110→You can select calculated expressions and literal values:
   111→
   112→```cpp
   113→struct Result {
   114→    std::string field;
   115→    double avg_field2;
   116→    std::optional<std::string> nullable_field;
   117→    int one;
   118→    std::string hello;
   119→};
   120→
   121→const auto query = select_from<TestTable>(
   122→    "field1"_c.as<"field">(),
   123→    avg("field2"_c).as<"avg_field2">(),
   124→    "nullable"_c | as<"nullable_field">,
   125→    as<"one">(1),                    // Literal value
   126→    "hello" | as<"hello">            // String literal
   127→) | to<Result>;
   128→```
   129→
   130→## Query Composition
   131→
   132→`select_from` can be combined with various query operations:
   133→
   134→```cpp
   135→const auto query = select_from<Person>(
   136→    "first_name"_c,
   137→    "last_name"_c,
   138→    "age"_c
   139→) 
   140→| where("age"_c >= 18)              // Filter results
   141→| order_by("last_name"_c, "first_name"_c)  // Order results
   142→| limit(10)                         // Limit number of results
   143→| to<std::vector<Person>>;          // Convert to container
   144→```
   145→
   146→### With Joins
   147→
   148→```cpp
   149→const auto query = select_from<Person, "t1">(
   150→    "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   151→    "first_name"_t3 | as<"first_name_child">,
   152→    avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t3) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
   153→)
   154→| inner_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2)
   155→| inner_join<Person, "t3">("id"_t3 == "child_id"_t2)
   156→| group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t3)
   157→| order_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t3)
   158→| to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   159→```
   160→
   161→## Result Type Conversion
   162→
   163→### Using `to<Container>`
   164→
   165→Convert query results to specific container types:
   166→
   167→```cpp
   168→// Convert to vector
   169→const auto people_vec = query | to<std::vector<Person>>;
   170→
   171→// Convert to single result (query must return exactly one row)
   172→const auto person = query | to<Person>;
   173→
   174→// Return as Range (lazy evaluation)
   175→const auto people_range = query;  // Returns Range<...> by default
   176→```
   177→
   178→### Automatic Type Deduction
   179→
   180→If you don't specify `to<...>`, `select_from` returns a `Range` type that can be iterated:
   181→
   182→```cpp
   183→const auto query = select_from<Person>("first_name"_c, "age"_c);
   184→
   185→// Execute and iterate
   186→for (const auto& result : sqlite::connect().and_then(query).value()) {
   187→    if (result) {
   188→        std::cout << result->first_name << ": " << result->age << std::endl;
   189→    }
   190→}
   191→```
   192→
   193→## Syntax Variations
   194→
   195→### Three Main Forms
   196→
   197→1. **Table without alias:**
   198→   ```cpp
   199→   select_from<TableType>(fields...)
   200→   ```
   201→
   202→2. **Table with alias:**
   203→   ```cpp
   204→   select_from<TableType, "t1">(fields...)
   205→   ```
   206→
   207→3. **Subquery with alias:**
   208→   ```cpp
   209→   select_from<"t1">(subquery, fields...)
   210→   ```
   211→
   212→## Column References
   213→
   214→Use the predefined column literals for clean syntax:
   215→
   216→```cpp
   217→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   218→
   219→// Use _c for unaliased tables
   220→"column_name"_c
   221→
   222→// Use _t1, _t2, etc. for aliased tables/joins
   223→"column_name"_t1, "column_name"_t2
   224→
   225→// Or use explicit col syntax
   226→col<"column_name", "t1">
   227→```
   228→
   229→## Advanced Examples
   230→
   231→### Complex Nested Query
   232→
   233→```cpp
   234→struct ParentAndChild {
   235→    std::string last_name;
   236→    std::string first_name_parent;
   237→    std::string first_name_child;
   238→    double parent_age_at_birth;
   239→};
   240→
   241→// Step 1: Create a subquery to get parent-child relationships
   242→const auto get_children = select_from<Relationship, "t1">(
   243→    "parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
   244→    "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
   245→    "age"_t2 | as<"age">
   246→) | inner_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
   247→
   248→// Step 2: Use the subquery in a larger query
   249→const auto get_people = select_from<Person, "t1">(
   250→    "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   251→    "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name_parent">,
   252→    "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
   253→    ("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"parent_age_at_birth">
   254→) 
   255→| inner_join<"t2">(get_children, "id"_t1 == "id"_t2)
   256→| order_by("id"_t1, "id"_t2)
   257→| to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   258→```
   259→
   260→### Aggregation with Grouping
   261→
   262→```cpp
   263→const auto summary = select_from<Person>(
   264→    "last_name"_c,
   265→    count() | as<"family_size">,
   266→    avg("age"_c) | as<"avg_age">,
   267→    min("age"_c) | as<"youngest">,
   268→    max("age"_c) | as<"oldest">
   269→) 
   270→| group_by("last_name"_c)
   271→| order_by("last_name"_c)
   272→| to<std::vector<FamilySummary>>;
   273→```
   274→
   275→## Important Notes
   276→
   277→- **Field Matching**: Result struct field names must exactly match the aliases used in the query
   278→- **Type Safety**: All column references and types are checked at compile time
   279→- **Null Handling**: Use `std::optional<T>` for nullable columns in result types
   280→- **Execution**: Queries are executed when passed to a database connection
   281→- **Composition**: Queries can be built incrementally and reused as subqueries
   282→- **Aliases Required**: When using joins or subqueries, table aliases are mandatory for disambiguation and must follow the pattern `t1`, `t2`, `t3`, etc.
   283→
   284→## Error Handling
   285→
   286→Queries return `Result<T>` types that must be handled:
   287→
   288→```cpp
   289→const auto result = sqlite::connect()
   290→    .and_then(query)
   291→    .value();  // Throws on error
   292→
   293→// Or handle errors explicitly
   294→const auto result = sqlite::connect()
   295→    .and_then(query);
   296→    
   297→if (result) {
   298→    // Success
   299→    use_data(*result);
   300→} else {
   301→    // Handle error
   302→    std::cerr << "Query failed: " << result.error().what() << std::endl;
   303→}
   304→```
   305→

1→# `sqlgen::inner_join`, `sqlgen::left_join`, `sqlgen::right_join`, `sqlgen::full_join`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen` library provides a type-safe, composable interface for expressing SQL joins in C++. It supports all standard SQL join types (inner, left, right, full) and allows for both simple and nested join queries, including joining on subqueries.
     4→
     5→## Join Types
     6→
     7→The following join types are available:
     8→
     9→- `inner_join` — Returns rows when there is a match in both tables
    10→- `left_join` — Returns all rows from the left table, and matched rows from the right table
    11→- `right_join` — Returns all rows from the right table, and matched rows from the left table
    12→- `full_join` — Returns all rows when there is a match in one of the tables (not supported by MariaDB)
    13→
    14→Each join type can be used with either a table or a subquery, and can be aliased for use in complex queries.
    15→
    16→## Usage
    17→
    18→### Basic Join Example
    19→
    20→```cpp
    21→using namespace sqlgen;
    22→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    23→
    24→struct Person {
    25→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id;
    26→    std::string first_name;
    27→    std::string last_name;
    28→    double age;
    29→};
    30→
    31→struct Relationship {
    32→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> parent_id;
    33→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> child_id;
    34→};
    35→
    36→// Join two tables: Relationship (as t1) and Person (as t2)
    37→const auto get_children =
    38→    select_from<Relationship, "t1">(
    39→        "parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
    40→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
    41→        "age"_t2 | as<"age">
    42→    ) |
    43→    left_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
    44→```
    45→
    46→This produces a query equivalent to:
    47→
    48→```sql
    49→SELECT t1."parent_id" AS "id", t2."first_name" AS "first_name", t2."age" AS "age"
    50→FROM "Relationship" t1
    51→LEFT JOIN "Person" t2 ON t2."id" = t1."child_id"
    52→```
    53→
    54→### Chaining Multiple Joins
    55→
    56→You can chain multiple joins to build more complex queries:
    57→
    58→```cpp
    59→const auto get_people =
    60→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
    61→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
    62→        "first_name"_t3 | as<"first_name_child">,
    63→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t3) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
    64→    ) |
    65→    inner_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2) |
    66→    left_join<Person, "t3">("id"_t3 == "child_id"_t2) |
    67→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t3) |
    68→    order_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t3) |
    69→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
    70→```
    71→
    72→This produces a query with both an inner and a left join, grouping and ordering the results.
    73→
    74→### Nested Joins and Subqueries
    75→
    76→`sqlgen` allows you to join on subqueries, enabling nested join patterns:
    77→
    78→```cpp
    79→const auto get_children =
    80→    select_from<Relationship, "t1">(
    81→        "parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
    82→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
    83→        "age"_t2 | as<"age">
    84→    ) |
    85→    left_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
    86→
    87→const auto get_people =
    88→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
    89→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
    90→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
    91→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
    92→    ) |
    93→    inner_join<"t2">(get_children, "id"_t1 == "id"_t2) |
    94→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t2) |
    95→    order_by("first_name"_t2) |
    96→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
    97→```
    98→
    99→This produces a query with a subquery in the join clause:
   100→
   101→```sql
   102→SELECT t1."last_name" AS "last_name", t2."first_name" AS "first_name_child", AVG((t1."age") - (t2."age")) AS "avg_parent_age_at_birth"
   103→FROM "Person" t1
   104→INNER JOIN (
   105→    SELECT t1."parent_id" AS "id", t2."first_name" AS "first_name", t2."age" AS "age"
   106→    FROM "Relationship" t1
   107→    INNER JOIN "Person" t2 ON t2."id" = t1."child_id"
   108→) t2 ON t1."id" = t2."id"
   109→GROUP BY t1."last_name", t2."first_name"
   110→ORDER BY t2."first_name"
   111→```
   112→
   113→## Join Syntax
   114→
   115→- `inner_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Inner join with a table
   116→- `left_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Left join with a table
   117→- `right_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Right join with a table
   118→- `full_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Full join with a table
   119→- `inner_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Inner join with a subquery
   120→- `left_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Left join with a subquery
   121→- `right_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Right join with a subquery
   122→- `full_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Full join with a subquery
   123→
   124→Where:
   125→- `Table` is the C++ struct representing the table
   126→- `Alias` is a string literal alias for the table or subquery
   127→- `condition` is a boolean expression relating columns from the joined tables
   128→- `subquery` is a previously constructed query expression
   129→
   130→## Aliasing and Column References
   131→
   132→When joining tables or subqueries, you must use aliases to disambiguate columns. Use the `_t1`, `_t2`, etc. 
   133→suffixes to refer to columns from different tables or subqueries, which are defined in the 
   134→namespace `sqlgen::literals`:
   135→
   136→```cpp
   137→"id"_t1, "first_name"_t2, "age"_t3
   138→```
   139→
   140→The library includes predefined suffixes from `_t1` to `_t99`.
   141→
   142→If you want to use your own alias, you can use this syntax instead:
   143→
   144→```cpp
   145→col<"id", "your_alias">, col<"first_name", "your_alias">, col<"age", "your_alias">
   146→```
   147→
   148→## Advanced: Nested and Grouped Joins
   149→
   150→You can nest joins and combine them with grouping and aggregation:
   151→
   152→```cpp
   153→const auto get_people =
   154→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   155→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   156→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
   157→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
   158→    ) |
   159→    inner_join<"t2">(get_children, "id"_t1 == "id"_t2) |
   160→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t2) |
   161→    order_by("first_name"_t2) |
   162→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   163→```
   164→
   165→## Nullability in Joins
   166→
   167→When performing outer joins (`left_join`, `right_join`, `full_join`), columns from the joined table may contain `NULL` values if no matching row is found. `sqlgen` handles this by wrapping the type of such columns in `std::optional`. If a field is already nullable (i.e., `std::optional<T>`), it remains `std::optional<T>`.
   168→
   169→-   `inner_join`: Does not introduce nullability. The types of the selected columns remain unchanged.
   170→-   `left_join`: Columns selected from the right table (the one being joined) will become `std::optional<T>` if they are not already nullable.
   171→-   `right_join`: Columns selected from the left table (the `select_from` table) will become `std::optional<T>` if they are not already nullable.
   172→-   `full_join`: Columns selected from both tables will become `std::optional<T>` if they are not already nullable.
   173→
   174→### Example: Nullability in a `left_join`
   175→
   176→Consider a `left_join` between `Person` and `Relationship` tables. If a person has no corresponding relationship, the columns from `Relationship` will be `NULL`.
   177→
   178→```cpp
   179→struct PersonWithOptionalRelationship {
   180→    uint32_t id;
   181→    std::string first_name;
   182→    std::optional<uint32_t> child_id;
   183→};
   184→
   185→const auto get_people_with_optional_relationship =
   186→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   187→        "id"_t1 | as<"id">,
   188→        "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name">,
   189→        "child_id"_t2 | as<"child_id">
   190→    ) |
   191→    left_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2) |
   192→    to<std::vector<PersonWithOptionalRelationship>>;
   193→```
   194→
   195→In this example, `child_id` is selected from the right table (`Relationship`) of a `left_join`. Therefore, its type in the result struct `PersonWithOptionalRelationship` must be `std::optional<uint32_t>` to handle cases where no matching relationship is found.
   196→
   197→### Nullability in Multi-Table Joins
   198→
   199→Nullability propagates through chained joins. If a table becomes nullable due to an outer join, any subsequent joins that use columns from that table will also treat them as nullable.
   200→
   201→For example, consider a query that joins `Person` to `Relationship` (left join) and then `Relationship` to a hypothetical `Pet` table (left join).
   202→
   203→```cpp
   204→struct PersonWithPets {
   205→    uint32_t person_id;
   206→    std::optional<uint32_t> child_id;
   207→    std::optional<std::string> pet_name;
   208→};
   209→
   210→// Assume Pet table has { id, name, owner_id }
   211→const auto get_people_with_pets =
   212→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   213→        "id"_t1 | as<"person_id">,
   214→        "child_id"_t2 | as<"child_id">,
   215→        "name"_t3 | as<"pet_name">
   216→    ) |
   217→    left_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2) |
   218→    left_join<Pet, "t3">("child_id"_t2 == "owner_id"_t3) | // Joining on a nullable-prone column
   219→    to<std::vector<PersonWithPets>>;
   220→```
   221→
   222→In this query:
   223→1.  The first `left_join` makes columns from `Relationship` (`t2`) nullable. So, `child_id` becomes `std::optional<uint32_t>`.
   224→2.  The second `left_join` joins `Pet` (`t3`). Since `t3` is on the right side of a `left_join`, its columns (like `pet_name`) also become nullable, resulting in `std::optional<std::string>`.
   225→
   226→If an `inner_join` were used for the second join (`Pet`), `pet_name` would still be `std::optional<std::string>` if the `Pet` table itself has a nullable `name` column. However, the join logic itself wouldn't introduce nullability for the `Pet` table's columns. The key principle is that the nullability of a column in the final result depends on both its original type and the types of joins applied to its table.
   227→
   228→## Notes
   229→
   230→- Joins can be chained and nested arbitrarily
   231→- Aliases are required for all joined tables and subqueries
   232→- Join conditions must use the correct aliases for columns
   233→- You can join on subqueries, enabling powerful query composition
   234→- Joins can be combined with `group_by`, `order_by`, and aggregation functions
   235→- The result type must match the structure of your select statement, with field names matching the aliases used in the query
   236→
   237→## Example: Full Nested Join Query
   238→
   239→```cpp
   240→struct ParentAndChild {
   241→    std::string last_name;
   242→    std::string first_name_child;
   243→    double avg_parent_age_at_birth;
   244→};
   245→
   246→const auto get_children =
   247→    select_from<Relationship, "t1">("parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
   248→                                    "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
   249→                                    "age"_t2 | as<"age">) |
   250→    inner_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
   251→
   252→const auto get_people =
   253→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   254→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   255→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
   256→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
   257→    ) |
   258→    inner_join<"t2">(get_children, "id"_t1 == "id"_t2) |
   259→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t2) |
   260→    order_by("first_name"_t2) |
   261→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   262→```
   263→
   264→This query joins a table to a subquery, groups by two columns, and computes an aggregate over the join.
   265→

1→# `sqlgen::sqlite`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::sqlite` module provides a type-safe and efficient interface for interacting with SQLite databases. It implements the core database operations through a connection-based API with support for prepared statements, transactions, and efficient data iteration.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Connection
     8→
     9→Create a connection to a SQLite database:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→// Connect to an in-memory database
    13→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect();
    14→
    15→// Connect to a file-based database
    16→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
    17→```
    18→
    19→The connection is wrapped in a `sqlgen::Result<Ref<Connection>>` for error handling:
    20→
    21→```cpp
    22→// Handle connection errors
    23→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
    24→if (!conn) {
    25→    // Handle error...
    26→    return;
    27→}
    28→
    29→using namespace sqlgen;
    30→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    31→
    32→const auto query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>> |
    33→                   where("age"_c < 18 and "first_name"_c != "Hugo");
    34→
    35→// Use the connection
    36→const auto minors = query(conn);
    37→```
    38→
    39→## Notes
    40→
    41→- The module provides a type-safe interface for SQLite operations
    42→- All operations return `sqlgen::Result<T>` for error handling
    43→- Prepared statements are used for efficient query execution
    44→- The iterator interface supports batch processing of results
    45→- SQL generation adapts to SQLite's dialect
    46→- The module supports:
    47→  - In-memory and file-based databases
    48→  - Transactions
    49→  - Prepared statements
    50→  - Efficient batch operations
    51→  - Type-safe SQL generation
    52→  - Error handling through `Result<T>`
    53→  - Resource management through `Ref<T>`

1→# Views
     2→
     3→sqlgen supports creating and managing database views, which are virtual tables based on the result set of a SQL statement. Views provide a way to simplify complex queries, present data in a specific format, or restrict access to certain columns.
     4→
     5→## Defining Views
     6→
     7→To define a view in sqlgen, create a struct with the `is_view` flag:
     8→
     9→```cpp
    10→struct EmployeeView {
    11→  static constexpr bool is_view = true;
    12→  
    13→  std::string first_name;
    14→  std::string last_name;
    15→  std::string department;
    16→  int salary;
    17→};
    18→```
    19→
    20→### Custom View Names
    21→
    22→You can optionally specify a custom name for your view using either `viewname` or `tablename`:
    23→
    24→```cpp
    25→struct EmployeeView {
    26→  static constexpr const char* viewname = "EMPLOYEE_SUMMARY";  // or tablename = "EMPLOYEE_SUMMARY"
    27→  static constexpr bool is_view = true;
    28→  
    29→  std::string first_name;
    30→  std::string last_name;
    31→  std::string department;
    32→  int salary;
    33→};
    34→```
    35→
    36→Both `viewname` and `tablename` work identically for views - they are just syntactic sugar.
    37→
    38→## Creating Views
    39→
    40→### Basic View Creation
    41→
    42→Create a view from a SELECT query:
    43→
    44→```cpp
    45→using namespace sqlgen;
    46→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    47→
    48→const auto employee_query = select_from<Employee>("first_name"_c, "last_name"_c, "department"_c, "salary"_c);
    49→const auto create_view = create_as<EmployeeView>(employee_query);
    50→
    51→create_view(conn).value();
    52→```
    53→
    54→This generates:
    55→
    56→```sql
    57→CREATE VIEW "EmployeeView" AS SELECT "first_name", "last_name", "department", "salary" FROM "Employee";
    58→```
    59→
    60→### Create or Replace View
    61→
    62→Use `create_or_replace_view_as` to create a view or replace it if it already exists:
    63→
    64→```cpp
    65→const auto employee_query = select_from<Employee>("first_name"_c, "last_name"_c, "department"_c, "salary"_c);
    66→const auto create_view = create_or_replace_view_as<EmployeeView>(employee_query);
    67→
    68→create_view(conn).value();
    69→```
    70→
    71→This generates different SQL depending on the database:
    72→
    73→- **MySQL/PostgreSQL**: `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW "EMPLOYEE_SUMMARY" AS SELECT ...`
    74→- **SQLite**: `CREATE VIEW "EmployeeView" AS SELECT ...`
    75→
    76→**Important**: SQLite does not support `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW`. When you use `create_or_replace_view_as` with SQLite, sqlgen does not automatically translate this and will result in an error if the view already exists. The recommended way to achieve this is to manually drop the view before creating it:
    77→
    78→```cpp
    79→(drop<EmployeeView> | if_exists)(conn).value();
    80→const auto create_view = create_as<EmployeeView>(employee_query);
    81→create_view(conn).value();
    82→```
    83→
    84→### View Creation with if_not_exists
    85→
    86→For SQLite compatibility, you can also use the `if_not_exists` modifier:
    87→
    88→```cpp
    89→const auto employee_query = select_from<Employee>("first_name"_c, "last_name"_c, "department"_c, "salary"_c);
    90→const auto create_view = create_as<EmployeeView>(employee_query) | if_not_exists;
    91→
    92→create_view(conn).value();
    93→```
    94→
    95→This generates different SQL depending on the database:
    96→
    97→- **SQLite**: `CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS "EmployeeView" AS SELECT ...`
    98→- **MySQL/PostgreSQL**: `CREATE VIEW "EmployeeView" AS SELECT ...` (if_not_exists ignored for views)
    99→
   100→## Complex View Examples
   101→
   102→### Filtered Views
   103→
   104→Create views with WHERE clauses:
   105→
   106→```cpp
   107→struct HighSalaryEmployees {
   108→  static constexpr bool is_view = true;
   109→  
   110→  std::string first_name;
   111→  std::string last_name;
   112→  int salary;
   113→};
   114→
   115→const auto high_salary_query = select_from<Employee>("first_name"_c, "last_name"_c, "salary"_c) |
   116→                               where("salary"_c > 50000);
   117→
   118→const auto create_high_salary_view = create_or_replace_view_as<HighSalaryEmployees>(high_salary_query);
   119→```
   120→
   121→### Joined Views
   122→
   123→Create views from joined tables:
   124→
   125→```cpp
   126→struct EmployeeDepartment {
   127→  static constexpr bool is_view = true;
   128→  
   129→  std::string first_name;
   130→  std::string last_name;
   131→  std::string department_name;
   132→  std::string location;
   133→};
   134→
   135→const auto joined_query = select_from<Employee, "t1">(
   136→    "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name">,
   137→    "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   138→    "department_name"_t2 | as<"department_name">,
   139→    "location"_t2 | as<"location">
   140→) |
   141→inner_join<Department, "t2">("department_id"_t1 == "id"_t2);
   142→
   143→const auto create_joined_view = create_or_replace_view_as<EmployeeDepartment>(joined_query);
   144→```
   145→
   146→### Aggregated Views
   147→
   148→Create views with aggregations:
   149→
   150→```cpp
   151→struct DepartmentStats {
   152→  static constexpr bool is_view = true;
   153→  
   154→  std::string department;
   155→  int employee_count;
   156→  double avg_salary;
   157→  int total_salary;
   158→};
   159→
   160→const auto stats_query = select_from<Employee>(
   161→                            "department"_c,
   162→                            count("id"_c) | as<"employee_count">,
   163→                            avg("salary"_c) | as<"avg_salary">,
   164→                            sum("salary"_c) | as<"total_salary">
   165→                        ) | group_by("department"_c);
   166→
   167→const auto create_stats_view = create_or_replace_view_as<DepartmentStats>(stats_query);
   168→```
   169→
   170→## Working with Views
   171→
   172→### Reading from Views
   173→
   174→Views can be used just like regular tables:
   175→
   176→```cpp
   177→// Read all data from the view
   178→const auto employees = sqlgen::read<std::vector<EmployeeView>>(conn).value();
   179→
   180→// Query the view with conditions
   181→const auto high_earners_query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<EmployeeView>> | where("salary"_c > 75000);
   182→const auto high_earners = high_earners_query(conn).value();
   183→```
   184→
   185→### Dropping Views
   186→
   187→Drop views using the same `drop` interface:
   188→
   189→```cpp
   190→using namespace sqlgen;
   191→
   192→const auto result = drop<EmployeeView>(conn);
   193→// or with if_exists
   194→const auto result = (drop<EmployeeView> | if_exists)(conn);
   195→```
   196→
   197→## Database-Specific Behavior
   198→
   199→### MySQL and PostgreSQL
   200→
   201→Both MySQL and PostgreSQL support `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW`:
   202→
   203→```sql
   204→CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW "EMPLOYEE_SUMMARY" AS SELECT ...;
   205→```
   206→
   207→### SQLite
   208→
   209→SQLite has different view creation behavior. It does not support `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW`. Instead, you should manually drop the view if it exists before creating it. See the example in the "Create or Replace View" section.
   210→
   211→## Best Practices
   212→
   213→1. **Naming Convention**: Use descriptive names for views that indicate their purpose
   214→2. **Column Selection**: Only include columns that are actually needed in the view
   215→3. **Performance**: Views with complex joins or aggregations may impact query performance
   216→4. **Maintenance**: Keep views simple and focused on a single purpose
   217→5. **Documentation**: Document the purpose and expected data of each view
   218→6. **Database Compatibility**: Be aware of database-specific differences in view creation syntax
   219→7. **SQLite Users**: Use `create_as<ViewType>(query) | if_not_exists` for better compatibility
   220→
   221→## Notes
   222→
   223→- Views are read-only by default in most databases
   224→- Views can be used in other queries just like regular tables

1→# `sqlgen::group_by` and Aggregations
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::group_by` interface provides a type-safe way to group and aggregate data in SQL queries. It supports various aggregation functions like `count`, `avg`, `sum`, `min`, `max`, and `count_distinct`.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Aggregations
     8→
     9→Perform aggregations without grouping:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→using namespace sqlgen;
    13→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    14→
    15→struct Children {
    16→    int num_children;
    17→    int num_last_names;
    18→    double avg_age;
    19→    double max_age;
    20→    double min_age;
    21→    double sum_age;
    22→};
    23→
    24→const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
    25→    avg("age"_c).as<"avg_age">(),
    26→    count().as<"num_children">(),
    27→    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),
    28→    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),
    29→    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),
    30→    count_distinct("last_name"_c).as<"num_last_names">()
    31→) | where("age"_c < 18) | to<Children>;
    32→
    33→const auto children = sqlite::connect()
    34→    .and_then(get_children)
    35→    .value();
    36→```
    37→
    38→This generates the following SQL:
    39→
    40→```sql
    41→SELECT 
    42→    AVG("age") as "avg_age",
    43→    COUNT(*) as "num_children",
    44→    MAX("age") as "max_age",
    45→    MIN("age") as "min_age",
    46→    SUM("age") as "sum_age",
    47→    COUNT(DISTINCT "last_name") as "num_last_names"
    48→FROM "Person"
    49→WHERE "age" < 18;
    50→```
    51→
    52→### Group By with Aggregations
    53→
    54→Group data and perform aggregations:
    55→
    56→```cpp
    57→using namespace sqlgen;
    58→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    59→
    60→struct Children {
    61→    std::string last_name;
    62→    int num_children;
    63→    int num_last_names;
    64→    double avg_age;
    65→    double max_age;
    66→    double min_age;
    67→    double sum_age;
    68→};
    69→
    70→const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
    71→    "last_name"_c,
    72→    avg("age"_c).as<"avg_age">(),
    73→    count().as<"num_children">(),
    74→    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),
    75→    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),
    76→    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),
    77→    count_distinct("last_name"_c).as<"num_last_names">()
    78→) | where("age"_c < 18) | group_by("last_name"_c) | to<std::vector<Children>>;
    79→
    80→const auto children = sqlite::connect()
    81→    .and_then(drop<Person> | if_exists)
    82→    .and_then(write(std::ref(people)))
    83→    .and_then(get_children)
    84→    .value();
    85→```
    86→
    87→This generates the following SQL:
    88→
    89→```sql
    90→SELECT 
    91→    "last_name",
    92→    AVG("age") as "avg_age",
    93→    COUNT(*) as "num_children",
    94→    MAX("age") as "max_age",
    95→    MIN("age") as "min_age",
    96→    SUM("age") as "sum_age",
    97→    COUNT(DISTINCT "last_name") as "num_last_names"
    98→FROM "Person"
    99→WHERE "age" < 18
   100→GROUP BY "last_name";
   101→```
   102→
   103→## Available Aggregation Functions
   104→
   105→The following aggregation functions are available:
   106→
   107→- `count()` - Counts all rows
   108→- `count_distinct(col)` - Counts distinct values in a column
   109→- `avg(col)` - Calculates average of a column
   110→- `sum(col)` - Calculates sum of a column
   111→- `max(col)` - Finds maximum value in a column
   112→- `min(col)` - Finds minimum value in a column
   113→
   114→Each aggregation function can be aliased using the `.as<"alias">()` syntax.
   115→
   116→## Aggregating Nullable Values
   117→
   118→When working with nullable columns (e.g., `std::optional<T>`), it's important to understand how aggregations handle null values:
   119→
   120→1. The result of aggregating a nullable column must also be nullable (e.g., `std::optional<double>`)
   121→2. Null values are excluded from aggregation calculations
   122→3. If all values in a group are null, the aggregation result will be null
   123→
   124→### Example with Nullable Values
   125→
   126→```cpp
   127→struct Person {
   128→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id;
   129→    std::string first_name;
   130→    std::string last_name;
   131→    std::optional<double> age;  // Nullable age field
   132→};
   133→
   134→struct Children {
   135→    int num_children;           // Non-nullable count
   136→    int num_last_names;        // Non-nullable count
   137→    std::optional<double> avg_age;  // Nullable aggregation
   138→    std::optional<double> max_age;  // Nullable aggregation
   139→    std::optional<double> min_age;  // Nullable aggregation
   140→    std::optional<double> sum_age;  // Nullable aggregation
   141→};
   142→
   143→const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
   144→    avg("age"_c).as<"avg_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
   145→    count().as<"num_children">(),      // Results in int (non-nullable)
   146→    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
   147→    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
   148→    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
   149→    count_distinct("last_name"_c).as<"num_last_names">()
   150→) | where("age"_c < 18 or "age"_c.is_null()) | to<Children>;
   151→```
   152→
   153→In this example:
   154→- The `age` column is nullable (`std::optional<double>`)
   155→- All aggregations of `age` result in nullable values (`std::optional<double>`)
   156→- The `count()` and `count_distinct()` functions return non-nullable integers
   157→- The `where` clause includes both non-null values less than 18 and null values
   158→- If all values in a group are null, the aggregation results (avg, max, min, sum) will be null
   159→
   160→### Important Notes
   161→
   162→- Always use nullable types (`std::optional<T>`) for aggregated values when the source column is nullable
   163→- Count operations (`count()`, `count_distinct()`) always return non-nullable integers
   164→- Null values are excluded from aggregation calculations (avg, sum, max, min)
   165→- When all values in a group are null, the aggregation result will be null
   166→- The type system will enforce these rules at compile time
   167→
   168→## The `.as` Operator
   169→
   170→The `.as` operator allows you to alias columns and expressions in your SQL queries. This is particularly important when mapping query results to C++ structs, as the field names in your struct must match the aliases used in the query.
   171→
   172→### Usage
   173→
   174→You can use `.as` in several ways:
   175→
   176→```cpp
   177→// Method 1: Using the .as() member function
   178→"field1"_c.as<"field">()
   179→
   180→// Method 2: Using the pipe operator with as
   181→"nullable"_c | as<"nullable_field">
   182→
   183→// Method 3: Using as directly with values
   184→as<"one">(1)
   185→"hello" | as<"hello">
   186→```
   187→
   188→### Important Notes
   189→
   190→- Field names in your result struct must exactly match the aliases used in the query
   191→- Fields are matched by name, not by order
   192→- You can alias any column, expression, or literal value
   193→- The alias must be a string literal (using the `as<"alias">` syntax)
   194→
   195→### Example
   196→
   197→```cpp
   198→struct Result {
   199→    std::string field;           // Matches "field1"_c.as<"field">()
   200→    double avg_field2;           // Matches avg("field2"_c).as<"avg_field2">()
   201→    std::optional<std::string> nullable_field;  // Matches "nullable"_c | as<"nullable_field">
   202→    int one;                     // Matches as<"one">(1)
   203→    std::string hello;           // Matches "hello" | as<"hello">
   204→};
   205→
   206→const auto query = select_from<TestTable>(
   207→    "field1"_c.as<"field">(),
   208→    avg("field2"_c).as<"avg_field2">(),
   209→    "nullable"_c | as<"nullable_field">,
   210→    as<"one">(1),
   211→    "hello" | as<"hello">
   212→) | to<Result>;
   213→```
   214→
   215→In this example, each field in the `Result` struct must have a name that matches one of the aliases used in the query. The order of the fields in the struct doesn't matter, but the names must match exactly.
   216→
   217→## Notes
   218→
   219→- The `group_by` clause must be used before `order_by` or `limit` clauses
   220→- You cannot use `group_by` multiple times in the same query
   221→- Aggregation functions can be used with or without `group_by`
   222→- The result type must match the structure of your select statement. Note that fields are matched by name, not order.
   223→- All aggregations are type-safe and will map to appropriate SQL types
   224→- The `Result<...>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed

1→# `sqlgen::exec`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::exec` interface provides a way to execute raw SQL statements on a database connection. It's useful when you need to perform database operations that aren't covered by the type-safe interfaces, such as setting database-specific parameters or executing custom SQL statements.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Execution
     8→
     9→Execute a raw SQL statement:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→const auto conn = sqlgen::postgres::connect(credentials);
    13→
    14→sqlgen::exec(conn, "SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';").value();
    15→```
    16→
    17→### Curried Execution
    18→
    19→You can also use a curried version of `exec` that takes the SQL statement first and returns a function that accepts the connection. This is useful for chaining operations:
    20→
    21→```cpp
    22→using namespace sqlgen;
    23→
    24→const auto query = exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';");
    25→
    26→// Using with a connection reference
    27→const auto conn = postgres::connect(credentials);
    28→query(conn).value();
    29→
    30→// Or in a chain with other operations
    31→postgres::connect(credentials)
    32→    .and_then(exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';"))
    33→    .value();
    34→```
    35→
    36→## Example: Full Query Composition
    37→
    38→Here's a complete example showing how to use `exec` within a chain of operations:
    39→
    40→```cpp
    41→using namespace sqlgen;
    42→
    43→const auto result = postgres::connect(credentials)
    44→    .and_then(exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';"))
    45→    .and_then(drop<Person> | if_exists)
    46→    .and_then(write(people))
    47→    .and_then(read<std::vector<Person>>)
    48→    .value();
    49→```
    50→
    51→This executes the following SQL statements in sequence:
    52→
    53→```sql
    54→SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';
    55→DROP TABLE IF EXISTS "Person";
    56→-- Table creation and data insertion via write
    57→-- Data retrieval via read
    58→```
    59→
    60→## Notes
    61→
    62→- The `Result<Ref<Connection>>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed
    63→- The function has two overloads:
    64→  1. Takes a connection reference and SQL string
    65→  2. Takes a `Result<Ref<Connection>>` and SQL string
    66→- The curried version is particularly useful when you want to:
    67→  - Chain multiple database operations together
    68→  - Pass the execution operation as a function to other operations
    69→- Use `exec` when you need to:
    70→  - Execute database-specific commands
    71→  - Set database parameters
    72→  - Run custom SQL statements not covered by type-safe interfaces
    73→  - Perform administrative tasks
    74→- Exercise caution when using `exec` with user-provided input to prevent SQL injection attacks
    75→- The SQL statement is executed as-is, so ensure it's compatible with your database dialect

1→# `sqlgen::read` 
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::read` interface provides a flexible and type-safe way to query data from a SQL database into C++ containers or ranges. It supports composable query building with `where`, `order_by`, and `limit` clauses.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Read
     8→
     9→Read all rows from a table into a container (e.g., `std::vector<Person>`):
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
    13→
    14→const std::vector<Person> people = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>>(conn).value();
    15→```
    16→
    17→This generates the following SQL:
    18→
    19→```sql
    20→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age"
    21→FROM "Person";
    22→```
    23→
    24→Note that `conn` is actually a connection wrapped into an `sqlgen::Result<...>`.
    25→This means you can use monadic error handling and fit this into a single line:
    26→
    27→```cpp
    28→// sqlgen::Result<std::vector<Person>>
    29→const auto people = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db").and_then(
    30→                        sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>>);
    31→```
    32→
    33→Please refer to the documentation on `sqlgen::Result<...>` for more information on error handling.
    34→
    35→### With `where` clause
    36→
    37→Filter results using a `where` clause:
    38→
    39→```cpp
    40→using namespace sqlgen;
    41→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    42→
    43→const auto query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>> |
    44→                   where("age"_c < 18 and "first_name"_c != "Hugo");
    45→
    46→const auto minors = query(conn).value();
    47→```
    48→
    49→This generates the following SQL:
    50→
    51→```sql
    52→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age"
    53→FROM "Person"
    54→WHERE 
    55→    ("age" < 18) AND 
    56→    ("first_name" != 'Hugo');
    57→```
    58→
    59→Note that `"..."_c` refers to the name of the column. If such a field does not
    60→exists on the struct `Person`, the code will fail to compile. It is defined in 
    61→the namespace `sqlgen::literals`.
    62→
    63→You can also use monadic error handling here:
    64→
    65→```cpp
    66→using namespace sqlgen;
    67→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    68→
    69→const auto query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>> |
    70→                   where("age"_c < 18 and "first_name"_c != "Hugo");
    71→
    72→// sqlgen::Result<std::vector<Person>>
    73→const auto minors = sqlite::connect("database.db").and_then(query);
    74→```
    75→
    76→### With `order_by` and `limit`
    77→
    78→Sort and limit results:
    79→
    80→```cpp
    81→using namespace sqlgen;
    82→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    83→
    84→const auto query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>> |
    85→                   order_by("age"_c) |
    86→                   limit(2);
    87→
    88→const auto youngest_two = query(conn).value();
    89→```
    90→
    91→This generates the following SQL:
    92→
    93→```sql
    94→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age"
    95→FROM "Person"
    96→ORDER BY "age"
    97→LIMIT 2;
    98→```
    99→
   100→### With ranges
   101→
   102→Read results as a lazy range:
   103→
   104→```cpp
   105→const auto people_range = sqlgen::read<sqlgen::Range<Person>>(conn).value();
   106→
   107→for (const sqlgen::Result<Person>& person : people_range) {
   108→    // process result 
   109→}
   110→```
   111→
   112→`people_range` satisfies the `std::ranges::input_range` concept, making it compatible with C++20 ranges and views. This allows for memory-efficient iteration through database results and enables composition with other range operations:
   113→
   114→```cpp
   115→using namespace std::ranges::views;
   116→
   117→// Transform range results
   118→const auto first_names = people_range | transform([](const sqlgen::Result<Person>& r) {
   119→    return r.value().first_name;
   120→});
   121→
   122→// Filter range results
   123→const auto adults = people_range | filter([](const sqlgen::Result<Person>& r) {
   124→    return r && r->age >= 18;
   125→});
   126→```
   127→
   128→## Example: Full Query Composition
   129→
   130→```cpp
   131→using namespace sqlgen;
   132→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   133→
   134→const auto query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>> |
   135→                   where("age"_c >= 18) |
   136→                   order_by("last_name"_c, "first_name"_c.desc()) |
   137→                   limit(10);
   138→
   139→const auto adults = query(conn).value();
   140→```
   141→
   142→This generates the following SQL:
   143→
   144→```sql
   145→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age"
   146→FROM "Person"
   147→WHERE 
   148→    ("age" >= 18)
   149→ORDER BY 
   150→    "last_name",
   151→    "first_name" DESC
   152→LIMIT 10;
   153→```
   154→
   155→It is strongly recommended that you use `using namespace sqlgen` and `using namespace sqlgen::literals;`. However,
   156→if you do not want to do that, you can rewrite the example above as follows:
   157→
   158→```cpp
   159→const auto query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>> |
   160→                   sqlgen::where(sqlgen::col<"age"> >= 18) |
   161→                   sqlgen::order_by(sqlgen::col<"last_name">, sqlgen::col<"first_name">.desc()) |
   162→                   sqlgen::limit(10);
   163→
   164→const auto adults = query(conn).value();
   165→```
   166→
   167→## Notes
   168→
   169→- All query clauses (`where`, `order_by`, `limit`) are optional.
   170→- The `Result<ContainerType>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw a exception if the results) or handle errors as needed. Refer to the 
   171→- The `sqlgen::Range<T>` type allows for lazy iteration over results.
   172→- `"..."_c` refers to the name of the column.

1→# `sqlgen::select_from`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::select_from` function provides a type-safe, composable interface for building SQL SELECT queries in C++. It supports selecting from tables, subqueries, and complex nested queries with full support for joins, filtering, grouping, ordering, and result type conversion.
     4→
     5→## Basic Usage
     6→
     7→### Selecting from a Table
     8→
     9→```cpp
    10→using namespace sqlgen;
    11→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    12→
    13→struct Person {
    14→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id;
    15→    std::string first_name;
    16→    std::string last_name;
    17→    int age;
    18→};
    19→
    20→// Select specific columns
    21→const auto query = select_from<Person>("first_name"_c, "last_name"_c, "age"_c);
    22→
    23→// Execute the query
    24→const auto people = sqlite::connect()
    25→    .and_then(query | to<std::vector<Person>>)
    26→    .value();
    27→```
    28→
    29→This generates:
    30→```sql
    31→SELECT "first_name", "last_name", "age" FROM "Person"
    32→```
    33→
    34→### Selecting with Aliases
    35→
    36→Use aliases to rename columns in the result set:
    37→
    38→```cpp
    39→struct Result {
    40→    std::string name;
    41→    int person_age;
    42→};
    43→
    44→const auto query = select_from<Person>(
    45→    "first_name"_c | as<"name">,
    46→    "age"_c | as<"person_age">
    47→) | to<std::vector<Result>>;
    48→```
    49→
    50→This generates:
    51→```sql
    52→SELECT "first_name" AS "name", "age" AS "person_age" FROM "Person"
    53→```
    54→
    55→## Table Aliases
    56→
    57→### Aliased Tables
    58→
    59→When you need to reference the same table multiple times or want cleaner column references:
    60→
    61→```cpp
    62→const auto query = select_from<Person, "t1">(
    63→    "first_name"_t1,
    64→    "last_name"_t1,
    65→    "age"_t1
    66→) | where("age"_t1 > 18);
    67→```
    68→
    69→This generates:
    70→```sql
    71→SELECT t1."first_name", t1."last_name", t1."age" FROM "Person" t1 WHERE t1."age" > 18
    72→```
    73→
    74→## Selecting from Subqueries
    75→
    76→You can use the result of one query as the source for another query:
    77→
    78→```cpp
    79→// First, create a subquery
    80→const auto get_parents = select_from<Person, "t1">(
    81→    "child_id"_t2 | as<"id">,
    82→    "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name">,
    83→    "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
    84→    "age"_t1 | as<"age">
    85→) | inner_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2);
    86→
    87→// Then use it as a source for another query
    88→const auto get_people = select_from<"t1">(
    89→    get_parents,  // Use the subquery as the source
    90→    "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
    91→    "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name_parent">,
    92→    "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
    93→    ("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"parent_age_at_birth">
    94→) | inner_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t1 == "id"_t2);
    95→```
    96→
    97→This generates:
    98→```sql
    99→SELECT t1."last_name" AS "last_name", t1."first_name" AS "first_name_parent", t2."first_name" AS "first_name_child", (t1."age") - (t2."age") AS "parent_age_at_birth"

1→# Defining tables
     2→
     3→`sqlgen` provides a type-safe way to define database tables using C++ structs. It automatically handles table creation, schema management, and nullability through C++ types.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Table Definition
     8→
     9→Define a table using a simple C++ struct:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→struct People {
    13→    std::string first_name;
    14→    std::string last_name;
    15→    uint age;
    16→};
    17→```
    18→
    19→When you write data to this table, it will be automatically created if it doesn't exist:
    20→
    21→```cpp
    22→const auto people = std::vector<People>(...);
    23→const auto result = sqlgen::write(conn, people);
    24→```
    25→
    26→This generates SQL similar to:
    27→
    28→```sql
    29→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "People"(
    30→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
    31→    "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
    32→    "age" INTEGER NOT NULL
    33→);
    34→```
    35→
    36→### Custom Table Names
    37→
    38→Override the default table name using a static member:
    39→
    40→```cpp
    41→struct People {
    42→    constexpr static const char* tablename = "PEOPLE";
    43→    
    44→    std::string first_name;
    45→    std::string last_name;
    46→    uint age;
    47→};
    48→```
    49→
    50→This generates SQL with the custom table name:
    51→
    52→```sql
    53→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "PEOPLE"(
    54→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
    55→    "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
    56→    "age" INTEGER NOT NULL
    57→);
    58→```
    59→
    60→### Custom Schemas
    61→
    62→Define a table within a specific schema:
    63→
    64→```cpp
    65→struct People {
    66→    constexpr static const char* schema = "my_schema";
    67→    
    68→    std::string first_name;
    69→    std::string last_name;
    70→    uint age;
    71→};
    72→```
    73→
    74→This generates SQL with the schema specification:
    75→
    76→```sql
    77→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "my_schema"."People"(
    78→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
    79→    "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
    80→    "age" INTEGER NOT NULL
    81→);
    82→```
    83→
    84→### Nullable Fields
    85→
    86→As we have seen, all columns are non-nullable by default. But what if we do want
    87→nullability?
    88→
    89→As with reflect-cpp, `std::optional`, `std::shared_ptr` and `std::unique_ptr` are interpreted as nullable types,
    90→but it is strongly recommended that you use `std::optional`.
    91→
    92→So you can create nullable fields as follows:
    93→
    94→```cpp
    95→struct People {
    96→    rfl::PrimaryKey<std::string> first_name;
    97→    std::string last_name;
    98→    std::optional<uint> age;
    99→};
   100→```
   101→
   102→## Notes
   103→
   104→- All fields are non-nullable by default
   105→- Nullable fields can be defined using:
   106→  - `std::optional<T>` (strongly recommended)
   107→  - `std::shared_ptr<T>`
   108→  - `std::unique_ptr<T>`
   109→- Use `std::nullopt` or `nullptr` to represent NULL values
   110→- The exact SQL generated may vary between database dialects
   111→- Table names are inferred from struct names by default
   112→- Custom table names and schemas can be specified using static members

1→# `sqlgen::exec`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::exec` interface provides a way to execute raw SQL statements on a database connection. It's useful when you need to perform database operations that aren't covered by the type-safe interfaces, such as setting database-specific parameters or executing custom SQL statements.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Execution
     8→
     9→Execute a raw SQL statement:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→const auto conn = sqlgen::postgres::connect(credentials);
    13→
    14→sqlgen::exec(conn, "SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';").value();
    15→```
    16→
    17→### Curried Execution
    18→
    19→You can also use a curried version of `exec` that takes the SQL statement first and returns a function that accepts the connection. This is useful for chaining operations:
    20→
    21→```cpp
    22→using namespace sqlgen;
    23→
    24→const auto query = exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';");
    25→
    26→// Using with a connection reference
    27→const auto conn = postgres::connect(credentials);
    28→query(conn).value();
    29→
    30→// Or in a chain with other operations
    31→postgres::connect(credentials)
    32→    .and_then(exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';"))
    33→    .value();
    34→```
    35→
    36→## Example: Full Query Composition
    37→
    38→Here's a complete example showing how to use `exec` within a chain of operations:
    39→
    40→```cpp
    41→using namespace sqlgen;
    42→
    43→const auto result = postgres::connect(credentials)
    44→    .and_then(exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';"))
    45→    .and_then(drop<Person> | if_exists)
    46→    .and_then(write(people))
    47→    .and_then(read<std::vector<Person>>)
    48→    .value();
    49→```
    50→
    51→This executes the following SQL statements in sequence:
    52→
    53→```sql
    54→SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';
    55→DROP TABLE IF EXISTS "Person";
    56→-- Table creation and data insertion via write
    57→-- Data retrieval via read
    58→```
    59→
    60→## Notes
    61→
    62→- The `Result<Ref<Connection>>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed
    63→- The function has two overloads:
    64→  1. Takes a connection reference and SQL string
    65→  2. Takes a `Result<Ref<Connection>>` and SQL string
    66→- The curried version is particularly useful when you want to:
    67→  - Chain multiple database operations together
    68→  - Pass the execution operation as a function to other operations
    69→- Use `exec` when you need to:
    70→  - Execute database-specific commands
    71→  - Set database parameters
    72→  - Run custom SQL statements not covered by type-safe interfaces
    73→  - Perform administrative tasks
    74→- Exercise caution when using `exec` with user-provided input to prevent SQL injection attacks
    75→- The SQL statement is executed as-is, so ensure it's compatible with your database dialect

1→# `sqlgen::Timestamp`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::Timestamp` class provides a type-safe way to handle SQL timestamp fields in C++. It supports both regular timestamps and timestamps with time zones, with format validation at runtime. The class is essentially a wrapper around `std::tm` that adds format validation and SQL integration.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Definition
     8→
     9→Define a timestamp field in your struct with a specific format:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→struct Person {
    13→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id;
    14→    std::string first_name;
    15→    std::string last_name;
    16→    sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"> birthdate;  // Regular timestamp
    17→    sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S%z"> created_at;  // Timestamp with timezone
    18→};
    19→```
    20→
    21→This generates the following SQL schema:
    22→
    23→```sql
    24→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Person"(
    25→    "id" INTEGER NOT NULL,
    26→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
    27→    "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
    28→    "birthdate" TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    29→    "created_at" TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE NOT NULL,
    30→    PRIMARY KEY ("id")
    31→);
    32→```
    33→
    34→### Construction and Assignment
    35→
    36→Create and assign timestamp values:
    37→
    38→```cpp
    39→// Direct string assignment
    40→Person person{
    41→    .id = 1,
    42→    .first_name = "Homer",
    43→    .last_name = "Simpson",
    44→    .birthdate = "1989-12-17 12:00:00",
    45→    .created_at = "2024-03-20 15:30:00+0000"
    46→};
    47→
    48→// Create from std::tm
    49→std::tm birth_tm = std::tm{};
    50→birth_tm.tm_year = 89;  // Years since 1900
    51→birth_tm.tm_mon = 11;   // 0-11 for months
    52→birth_tm.tm_mday = 17;  // Day of month
    53→birth_tm.tm_hour = 12;
    54→birth_tm.tm_min = 0;
    55→birth_tm.tm_sec = 0;
    56→sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"> birthdate(birth_tm);
    57→
    58→// Safe construction with error handling
    59→auto result = sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S">::from_string("1989-12-17 12:00:00");
    60→if (result) {
    61→    auto birthdate = result.value();
    62→    // Use birthdate...
    63→} else {
    64→    // Handle error...
    65→}
    66→```
    67→
    68→### Accessing Values
    69→
    70→Access the timestamp value in different formats:
    71→

    83→
    84→### Time Zone Support
    85→
    86→The class supports both regular timestamps and timestamps with time zones:
    87→
    88→```cpp
    89→// Regular timestamp (without timezone)
    90→sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"> local_time;
    91→
    92→// Timestamp with timezone
    93→sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S%z"> utc_time;
    94→
    95→// Examples
    96→local_time = "2024-03-20 15:30:00";  // Local time
    97→utc_time = "2024-03-20 15:30:00+0000";  // UTC time with offset
    98→```
    99→
   100→## Format Specification
   101→
   102→The timestamp format is specified using a template parameter that follows the strftime format specifiers. This format is significant because:
   103→
   104→1. It defines the expected string format when reading timestamps from the database
   105→2. It determines how timestamps are formatted when writing to the database
   106→3. It enforces consistency between your C++ code and database storage
   107→
   108→For example, with this definition:
   109→```cpp
   110→struct Person {
   111→    sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"> birthdate;
   112→};
   113→```
   114→
   115→- When reading from the database, the timestamp must be in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS"
   116→- When writing to the database, the timestamp will be formatted as "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS"
   117→- Any attempt to assign a string in a different format will throw a runtime error
   118→
   119→The most importand supported format specifiers are:
   120→
   121→- `%Y`: Year with century (e.g., 2024)
   122→- `%m`: Month (01-12)
   123→- `%d`: Day of month (01-31)
   124→- `%H`: Hour in 24h format (00-23)
   125→- `%M`: Minute (00-59)
   126→- `%S`: Second (00-59)
   127→- `%z`: Timezone offset (e.g., +0000, -0500)
   128→
   129→Please refer to https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/chrono/c/strftime for a comprehensive list of supported format specifiers.
   130→
   131→Common format patterns:
   132→- `"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"` for regular timestamps
   133→- `"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S%z"` for timestamps with timezone
   134→
   135→### Database Integration
   136→
   137→The format parameter ensures type safety and consistency in database operations:
   138→
   139→```cpp
   140→// Reading from database

   147→};
   148→sqlgen::write(conn, person);  // Will be stored in the database in this format
   149→
   150→// Querying with timestamps
   151→const auto query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>> | 
   152→                  where("birthdate"_c == "1989-12-17 12:00:00");  // Must match the format
   153→```
   154→
   155→This format validation helps prevent:
   156→- Data corruption from inconsistent timestamp formats
   157→- SQL injection by validating the format before database operations
   158→- Runtime errors from malformed timestamp strings
   159→

   161→
   162→- The template parameter `_format` specifies the expected timestamp format
   163→- Format validation occurs at runtime when values are assigned

   165→  - Format validation
