1→# ![C++](https://img.shields.io/badge/c++-%2300599C.svg?style=for-the-badge&logo=c%2B%2B&logoColor=white) sqlgen 
     2→
     3→[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
     4→[![Maintenance](https://img.shields.io/badge/Maintained%3F-yes-green.svg)](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp/graphs/commit-activity)
     5→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/C++-20-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     6→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/gcc-11+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     7→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/clang-14+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     8→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/MSVC-17+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     9→
    10→**📖 Documentation**: [Click here](docs/README.md)
    11→
    12→**sqlgen** is a modern, type-safe ORM and SQL query generator for C++20, inspired by Python's [SQLAlchemy](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy)/[SQLModel](https://github.com/fastapi/sqlmodel) and Rust's [Diesel](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel). It provides a fluent, composable interface for database operations with compile-time type checking and SQL injection protection.
    13→
    14→sqlgen is based on and tightly integrated with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp), a C++-20 library for fast serialization, deserialization and validation using reflection, similar to pydantic in Python, serde in Rust, encoding in Go or aeson in Haskell.
    15→
    16→Together, reflect-cpp and sqlgen enable reliable and efficient ETL pipelines.
    17→
    18→## Features
    19→
    20→- 🔒 **Type Safety**: Compile-time validation of table schemas and queries
    21→- 🛡️ **SQL Injection Protection**: Built-in input validation and parameterized queries
    22→- 🔄 **Composable Queries**: Fluent interface for building complex queries
    23→- 🚀 **High Performance**: Efficient batch operations and prepared statements
    24→- 📦 **Modern C++**: Leverages C++20 features for a clean, expressive API
    25→- 🔌 **Multiple Backends**: Support for PostgreSQL and SQLite
    26→- 🔍 **Reflection Integration**: Seamless integration with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp) 
    27→
    28→## Supported databases 
    29→
    30→The following table lists the databases currently supported by sqlgen and the underlying libraries used:
    31→
    32→| Database      | Library                                                                  | Version      | License       | Remarks                                              |
    33→|---------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------|---------------| -----------------------------------------------------|
    34→| MySQL/MariaDB | [libmariadb](https://github.com/mariadb-corporation/mariadb-connector-c) | >= 3.4.5     | LGPL          |                                                      |
    35→| PostgreSQL    | [libpq](https://github.com/postgres/postgres)                            | >= 16.4      | PostgreSQL    | Will work for all libpq-compatible databases         |
    36→| sqlite        | [sqlite](https://sqlite.org/index.html)                                  | >= 3.49.1    | Public Domain |                                                      |
    37→
    38→## Quick Start
    39→
    40→### Installation using vcpkg
    41→
    42→1. Make sure you have the required dependencies installed (skip this step on Windows):
    43→```bash
    44→sudo apt-get install autoconf bison flex # Linux (Ubuntu, Debian, ...)
    45→brew install autoconf bison flex # macOS
    46→```
    47→
    48→2. Set up vcpkg:
    49→```bash
    50→git submodule update --init
    51→./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.sh  # Linux, macOS
    52→./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.bat # Windows
    53→```
    54→
    55→3. Build the library:
    56→```bash
    57→cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_CXX_STANDARD=20 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
    58→cmake --build build -j 4  # gcc, clang
    59→cmake --build build --config Release -j 4  # MSVC
    60→```
    61→
    62→This will build the static library. To build the shared library 
    63→add `-DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON -DVCPKG_TARGET_TRIPLET=...` to the first line.
    64→Run `./vcpkg/vcpkg help triplets` to view all supported triplets. 
    65→Common triplets for shared libraries are `x64-linux-dynamic`, 
    66→`arm64-osx-dynamic` or `x64-osx-dynamic`.   
    67→
    68→Add `-DSQLGEN_MYSQL=ON` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
    69→
    70→4. Include in your CMake project:
    71→```cmake
    72→find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)
    73→target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
    74→```
    75→
    76→### Installation using Conan
    77→
    78→1. Install Conan (assuming you have Python and pipx installed):
    79→
    80→```bash
    81→pipx install conan
    82→conan profile detect
    83→```
    84→
    85→For older versions of pip, you can also use `pip` instead of `pipx`.
    86→
    87→2. Build the library:
    88→
    89→```bash
    90→conan build . --build=missing -s compiler.cppstd=gnu20
    91→```
    92→
    93→This will build the static library. To build the shared library,
    94→add `-o */*:shared=True`. 
    95→
    96→Add `-o sqlgen/*:with_mysql=True` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
    97→
    98→3. Include in your CMake project:
    99→```cmake
   100→find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)
   101→target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
   102→```
   103→
   104→You can call `conan inspect .` to get an overview of the supported options.
   105→
   106→## Usage Examples
   107→
   108→### Hello World
   109→
   110→```cpp
   111→#include <sqlgen/sqlite.hpp>
   112→#include <iostream>
   113→
   114→struct User {
   115→    std::string name;
   116→    int age;
   117→};
   118→
   119→int main() {
   120→    // Connect to SQLite database
   121→    const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("test.db");
   122→    
   123→    // Create and insert a user
   124→    const auto user = User{.name = "John", .age = 30};
   125→    sqlgen::write(conn, user);
   126→    
   127→    // Read all users
   128→    const auto users = sqlgen::read<std::vector<User>>(conn).value();
   129→    
   130→    for (const auto& u : users) {
   131→        std::cout << u.name << " is " << u.age << " years old\n";
   132→    }
   133→}
   134→```
   135→
   136→### Connecting to a Database
   137→
   138→```cpp
   139→#include <sqlgen/postgres.hpp>
   140→
   141→// PostgreSQL connection
   142→const auto credentials = sqlgen::postgres::Credentials{
   143→    .user = "username",
   144→    .password = "password",
   145→    .host = "localhost",
   146→    .dbname = "mydb",
   147→    .port = 5432
   148→};
   149→
   150→const auto conn = sqlgen::postgres::connect(credentials);
   151→
   152→// SQLite connection
   153→const auto sqlite_conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
   154→```
   155→
   156→### Defining Models
   157→
   158→```cpp
   159→struct Person {
   160→    std::string first_name;
   161→    std::string last_name;
   162→    uint32_t age;
   163→    std::optional<std::string> email;  // Nullable field
   164→};
   165→```
   166→
   167→### Inserting Data
   168→
   169→```cpp
   170→const auto people = std::vector<Person>({
   171→    Person{.first_name = "Homer", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 45},
   172→    Person{.first_name = "Marge", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 42}
   173→});
   174→
   175→// Automatically creates table if it doesn't exist
   176→// (recall that the table is fully defined at compile time)
   177→const auto result = sqlgen::write(conn, people);
   178→
   179→if (!result) {
   180→    std::cerr << "Error: " << result.error().what() << std::endl;
   181→}
   182→```
   183→
   184→Or:
   185→
   186→```cpp
   187→...
   188→
   189→// write(...) abstracts these steps away, but
   190→// if you prefer more granular control, you
   191→// can use sqlgen::insert.
   192→const auto result = begin_transaction(conn)
   193→                        .and_then(create_table<Person> | if_not_exists)
   194→                        .and_then(insert(std::ref(people)))
   195→                        .and_then(commit);
   196→
   197→...
   198→```
   199→
   200→Generated SQL:
   201→```sql
   202→BEGIN TRANSACTION;
   203→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Person" (
   204→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
   205→    "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
   206→    "age" INTEGER NOT NULL,
   207→    "email" TEXT
   208→);
   209→
   210→INSERT INTO "Person" ("first_name", "last_name", "age", "email") 
   211→VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?);
   212→COMMIT;
   213→```
   214→
   215→### Querying Data
   216→
   217→```cpp
   218→#include <rfl/json.hpp>
   219→#include <sqlgen/postgres.hpp>
   220→
   221→using namespace sqlgen;
   222→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   223→
   224→// Build a query for adults, ordered by age
   225→const auto query = read<std::vector<Person>> |
   226→                   where("age"_c >= 18) |
   227→                   order_by("age"_c.desc(), "last_name"_c) |
   228→                   limit(10);
   229→
   230→// Execute the query
   231→const auto result = query(conn);
   232→
   233→if (result) {
   234→    // Print results as JSON
   235→    std::cout << rfl::json::write(*result) << std::endl;
   236→} else {
   237→    std::cerr << "Error: " << result.error().what() << std::endl;
   238→}
   239→```
   240→
   241→Generated SQL:
   242→```sql
   243→SELECT "first_name", "last_name", "age", "email"
   244→FROM "Person"
   245→WHERE "age" >= 18
   246→ORDER BY "age" DESC, "last_name"
   247→LIMIT 10;
   248→```
   249→
   250→### Grouping and Aggregating Data
   251→
   252→```cpp
   253→using namespace sqlgen;
   254→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   255→
   256→struct Children {
   257→    std::string last_name;
   258→    int num_children;
   259→    int max_age;
   260→    int min_age;
   261→    int sum_age;
   262→};
   263→
   264→const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
   265→    "last_name"_c,
   266→    count().as<"num_children">(),
   267→    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),
   268→    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),
   269→    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),
   270→) | where("age"_c < 18) | group_by("last_name"_c) | to<std::vector<Children>>;
   271→
   272→const std::vector<Children> children = get_children(conn).value();
   273→```

   279→    COUNT(*) as "num_children",
   280→    MAX("age") as "max_age",
   281→    MIN("age") as "min_age",
   282→    SUM("age") as "sum_age"
   283→FROM "Person"
   284→WHERE "age" < 18
   285→GROUP BY "last_name";

   294→struct ParentAndChild {

   296→    std::string first_name_parent;
   297→    std::string first_name_child;

   299→};

   309→  order_by("id"_t1, "id"_t3) | to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;

   317→       t1."age" - t3."age" AS "parent_age_at_birth" 
   318→FROM "Person" t1 
   319→INNER JOIN "Relationship" t2 
   320→ON t1."id" = t2."parent_id"

   429→### Type Safety and SQL Injection Protection
   430→
   431→sqlgen provides comprehensive compile-time checks and runtime protection:
   432→
   433→```cpp
   434→// Compile-time error: No such column "color"
   435→const auto query = read<std::vector<Person>> |
   436→                   where("color"_c == "blue");
   437→
   438→// Compile-time error: Cannot compare column "age" to a string 
   439→const auto query = read<std::vector<Person>> |
   440→                   where("age"_c == "Homer");
   441→
   442→// Compile-time error: "age" must be aggregated or included in GROUP BY 
   443→const auto query = select_from<Person>(
   444→    "last_name"_c,
   445→    "age"_c 
   446→) | group_by("last_name"_c);
   447→
   448→// Compile-time error: Cannot add string and int 
   449→const auto query = select_from<Person>(
   450→    "last_name"_c + "age"_c 
   451→);
   452→
   453→// Runtime protection against SQL injection
   454→std::vector<Person> get_people(const auto& conn, 
   455→                              const sqlgen::AlphaNumeric& first_name) {
   456→    using namespace sqlgen;
   457→    return (read<std::vector<Person>> | 
   458→            where("first_name"_c == first_name))(conn).value();

   462→get_people(conn, "Homer' OR '1'='1");  // SQL injection attempt

1→# `sqlgen::inner_join`, `sqlgen::left_join`, `sqlgen::right_join`, `sqlgen::full_join`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen` library provides a type-safe, composable interface for expressing SQL joins in C++. It supports all standard SQL join types (inner, left, right, full) and allows for both simple and nested join queries, including joining on subqueries.
     4→
     5→## Join Types
     6→
     7→The following join types are available:
     8→
     9→- `inner_join` — Returns rows when there is a match in both tables
    10→- `left_join` — Returns all rows from the left table, and matched rows from the right table
    11→- `right_join` — Returns all rows from the right table, and matched rows from the left table
    12→- `full_join` — Returns all rows when there is a match in one of the tables (not supported by MariaDB)
    13→
    14→Each join type can be used with either a table or a subquery, and can be aliased for use in complex queries.
    15→
    16→## Usage
    17→
    18→### Basic Join Example
    19→
    20→```cpp
    21→using namespace sqlgen;
    22→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    23→
    24→struct Person {
    25→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id;
    26→    std::string first_name;
    27→    std::string last_name;
    28→    double age;
    29→};
    30→
    31→struct Relationship {
    32→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> parent_id;
    33→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> child_id;
    34→};
    35→
    36→// Join two tables: Relationship (as t1) and Person (as t2)
    37→const auto get_children =
    38→    select_from<Relationship, "t1">(
    39→        "parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
    40→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
    41→        "age"_t2 | as<"age">
    42→    ) |
    43→    left_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
    44→```
    45→
    46→This produces a query equivalent to:
    47→
    48→```sql
    49→SELECT t1."parent_id" AS "id", t2."first_name" AS "first_name", t2."age" AS "age"
    50→FROM "Relationship" t1
    51→LEFT JOIN "Person" t2 ON t2."id" = t1."child_id"
    52→```
    53→
    54→### Chaining Multiple Joins
    55→
    56→You can chain multiple joins to build more complex queries:
    57→
    58→```cpp
    59→const auto get_people =
    60→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
    61→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
    62→        "first_name"_t3 | as<"first_name_child">,
    63→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t3) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
    64→    ) |
    65→    inner_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2) |
    66→    left_join<Person, "t3">("id"_t3 == "child_id"_t2) |
    67→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t3) |
    68→    order_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t3) |
    69→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
    70→```
    71→
    72→This produces a query with both an inner and a left join, grouping and ordering the results.
    73→
    74→### Nested Joins and Subqueries
    75→
    76→`sqlgen` allows you to join on subqueries, enabling nested join patterns:
    77→
    78→```cpp
    79→const auto get_children =
    80→    select_from<Relationship, "t1">(
    81→        "parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
    82→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
    83→        "age"_t2 | as<"age">
    84→    ) |
    85→    left_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
    86→
    87→const auto get_people =
    88→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
    89→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
    90→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
    91→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
    92→    ) |
    93→    inner_join<"t2">(get_children, "id"_t1 == "id"_t2) |
    94→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t2) |
    95→    order_by("first_name"_t2) |
    96→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
    97→```
    98→
    99→This produces a query with a subquery in the join clause:
   100→
   101→```sql
   102→SELECT t1."last_name" AS "last_name", t2."first_name" AS "first_name_child", AVG((t1."age") - (t2."age")) AS "avg_parent_age_at_birth"
   103→FROM "Person" t1
   104→INNER JOIN (
   105→    SELECT t1."parent_id" AS "id", t2."first_name" AS "first_name", t2."age" AS "age"
   106→    FROM "Relationship" t1
   107→    INNER JOIN "Person" t2 ON t2."id" = t1."child_id"
   108→) t2 ON t1."id" = t2."id"
   109→GROUP BY t1."last_name", t2."first_name"
   110→ORDER BY t2."first_name"
   111→```
   112→
   113→## Join Syntax
   114→
   115→- `inner_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Inner join with a table
   116→- `left_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Left join with a table
   117→- `right_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Right join with a table
   118→- `full_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Full join with a table
   119→- `inner_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Inner join with a subquery
   120→- `left_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Left join with a subquery
   121→- `right_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Right join with a subquery
   122→- `full_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Full join with a subquery
   123→
   124→Where:
   125→- `Table` is the C++ struct representing the table
   126→- `Alias` is a string literal alias for the table or subquery
   127→- `condition` is a boolean expression relating columns from the joined tables
   128→- `subquery` is a previously constructed query expression
   129→
   130→## Aliasing and Column References
   131→
   132→When joining tables or subqueries, you must use aliases to disambiguate columns. Use the `_t1`, `_t2`, etc. 
   133→suffixes to refer to columns from different tables or subqueries, which are defined in the 
   134→namespace `sqlgen::literals`:
   135→
   136→```cpp
   137→"id"_t1, "first_name"_t2, "age"_t3
   138→```
   139→
   140→The library includes predefined suffixes from `_t1` to `_t99`.
   141→
   142→If you want to use your own alias, you can use this syntax instead:
   143→
   144→```cpp
   145→col<"id", "your_alias">, col<"first_name", "your_alias">, col<"age", "your_alias">
   146→```
   147→
   148→## Advanced: Nested and Grouped Joins
   149→
   150→You can nest joins and combine them with grouping and aggregation:
   151→
   152→```cpp
   153→const auto get_people =
   154→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   155→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   156→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
   157→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
   158→    ) |
   159→    inner_join<"t2">(get_children, "id"_t1 == "id"_t2) |
   160→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t2) |
   161→    order_by("first_name"_t2) |
   162→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   163→```
   164→
   165→## Nullability in Joins
   166→
   167→When performing outer joins (`left_join`, `right_join`, `full_join`), columns from the joined table may contain `NULL` values if no matching row is found. `sqlgen` handles this by wrapping the type of such columns in `std::optional`. If a field is already nullable (i.e., `std::optional<T>`), it remains `std::optional<T>`.
   168→
   169→-   `inner_join`: Does not introduce nullability. The types of the selected columns remain unchanged.
   170→-   `left_join`: Columns selected from the right table (the one being joined) will become `std::optional<T>` if they are not already nullable.
   171→-   `right_join`: Columns selected from the left table (the `select_from` table) will become `std::optional<T>` if they are not already nullable.
   172→-   `full_join`: Columns selected from both tables will become `std::optional<T>` if they are not already nullable.
   173→
   174→### Example: Nullability in a `left_join`
   175→
   176→Consider a `left_join` between `Person` and `Relationship` tables. If a person has no corresponding relationship, the columns from `Relationship` will be `NULL`.
   177→
   178→```cpp
   179→struct PersonWithOptionalRelationship {
   180→    uint32_t id;
   181→    std::string first_name;
   182→    std::optional<uint32_t> child_id;
   183→};
   184→
   185→const auto get_people_with_optional_relationship =
   186→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   187→        "id"_t1 | as<"id">,
   188→        "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name">,
   189→        "child_id"_t2 | as<"child_id">
   190→    ) |
   191→    left_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2) |
   192→    to<std::vector<PersonWithOptionalRelationship>>;
   193→```
   194→
   195→In this example, `child_id` is selected from the right table (`Relationship`) of a `left_join`. Therefore, its type in the result struct `PersonWithOptionalRelationship` must be `std::optional<uint32_t>` to handle cases where no matching relationship is found.
   196→
   197→### Nullability in Multi-Table Joins
   198→
   199→Nullability propagates through chained joins. If a table becomes nullable due to an outer join, any subsequent joins that use columns from that table will also treat them as nullable.
   200→
   201→For example, consider a query that joins `Person` to `Relationship` (left join) and then `Relationship` to a hypothetical `Pet` table (left join).
   202→
   203→```cpp
   204→struct PersonWithPets {
   205→    uint32_t person_id;
   206→    std::optional<uint32_t> child_id;
   207→    std::optional<std::string> pet_name;
   208→};
   209→
   210→// Assume Pet table has { id, name, owner_id }
   211→const auto get_people_with_pets =
   212→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   213→        "id"_t1 | as<"person_id">,
   214→        "child_id"_t2 | as<"child_id">,
   215→        "name"_t3 | as<"pet_name">
   216→    ) |
   217→    left_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2) |
   218→    left_join<Pet, "t3">("child_id"_t2 == "owner_id"_t3) | // Joining on a nullable-prone column
   219→    to<std::vector<PersonWithPets>>;
   220→```
   221→
   222→In this query:
   223→1.  The first `left_join` makes columns from `Relationship` (`t2`) nullable. So, `child_id` becomes `std::optional<uint32_t>`.
   224→2.  The second `left_join` joins `Pet` (`t3`). Since `t3` is on the right side of a `left_join`, its columns (like `pet_name`) also become nullable, resulting in `std::optional<std::string>`.
   225→
   226→If an `inner_join` were used for the second join (`Pet`), `pet_name` would still be `std::optional<std::string>` if the `Pet` table itself has a nullable `name` column. However, the join logic itself wouldn't introduce nullability for the `Pet` table's columns. The key principle is that the nullability of a column in the final result depends on both its original type and the types of joins applied to its table.
   227→
   228→## Notes
   229→
   230→- Joins can be chained and nested arbitrarily
   231→- Aliases are required for all joined tables and subqueries
   232→- Join conditions must use the correct aliases for columns
   233→- You can join on subqueries, enabling powerful query composition
   234→- Joins can be combined with `group_by`, `order_by`, and aggregation functions
   235→- The result type must match the structure of your select statement, with field names matching the aliases used in the query
   236→
   237→## Example: Full Nested Join Query
   238→
   239→```cpp
   240→struct ParentAndChild {
   241→    std::string last_name;
   242→    std::string first_name_child;
   243→    double avg_parent_age_at_birth;
   244→};
   245→
   246→const auto get_children =
   247→    select_from<Relationship, "t1">("parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
   248→                                    "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
   249→                                    "age"_t2 | as<"age">) |
   250→    inner_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
   251→
   252→const auto get_people =
   253→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   254→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   255→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
   256→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
   257→    ) |
   258→    inner_join<"t2">(get_children, "id"_t1 == "id"_t2) |
   259→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t2) |
   260→    order_by("first_name"_t2) |
   261→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   262→```
   263→
   264→This query joins a table to a subquery, groups by two columns, and computes an aggregate over the join.
   265→

1→# `sqlgen::...::to_sql`
     2→
     3→The `to_sql` functions in each dialect namespace (e.g., `sqlgen::postgres::to_sql`, `sqlgen::sqlite::to_sql`) provide a way to transpile C++ SQL operations into dialect-specific SQL strings. This is particularly useful for testing, debugging, logging, and understanding the exact SQL that will be executed by sqlgen.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Usage
     8→
     9→Transpile any SQL operation to a dialect-specific SQL string:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→using namespace sqlgen;
    13→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    14→
    15→// Define a query
    16→const auto query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>> |
    17→                   where("age"_c < 18 and "first_name"_c != "Hugo") |
    18→                   order_by("age"_c);
    19→
    20→// Transpile to PostgreSQL dialect
    21→const auto postgres_sql = postgres::to_sql(query);
    22→```
    23→
    24→This generates the following PostgreSQL SQL:
    25→
    26→```sql
    27→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age" 
    28→FROM "Person" 
    29→WHERE ("age" < 18) AND ("first_name" != 'Hugo') 
    30→ORDER BY "age";
    31→```
    32→
    33→Or for SQLite:
    34→
    35→```cpp
    36→// Transpile to SQLite dialect
    37→const auto sqlite_sql = sqlite::to_sql(query);
    38→```
    39→
    40→### Supported Operations
    41→
    42→`to_sql` supports transpilation of all sqlgen operations:
    43→
    44→#### SELECT Queries
    45→
    46→```cpp
    47→using namespace sqlgen;
    48→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    49→
    50→// Basic select
    51→const auto select_query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>>;
    52→const auto sql = postgres::to_sql(select_query);
    53→```
    54→
    55→This generates the following SQL:
    56→
    57→```sql
    58→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age" 
    59→FROM "Person";
    60→```
    61→
    62→With a where clause:
    63→
    64→```cpp
    65→// With where clause
    66→const auto filtered_query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>> | 
    67→                           where("age"_c >= 18);
    68→const auto sql = postgres::to_sql(filtered_query);
    69→```
    70→
    71→This generates the following SQL:
    72→
    73→```sql
    74→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age" 
    75→FROM "Person" 
    76→WHERE "age" >= 18;
    77→```
    78→
    79→#### CREATE TABLE Operations
    80→
    81→Note that every call to `sqlgen::write` calls a `CREATE TABLE` operation
    82→before actually inserting the data.
    83→
    84→```cpp
    85→using namespace sqlgen;
    86→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    87→
    88→// Define a table structure
    89→struct TestTable {
    90→    std::string field1;
    91→    int32_t field2;
    92→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id;
    93→    std::optional<std::string> nullable;
    94→};
    95→
    96→// Create table query
    97→const auto create_query = create_table<TestTable> | if_not_exists;
    98→const auto sql = postgres::to_sql(create_query);
    99→```
   100→
   101→This generates the following PostgreSQL SQL:
   102→
   103→```sql
   104→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "TestTable" (
   105→    "field1" TEXT NOT NULL,
   106→    "field2" INTEGER NOT NULL,
   107→    "id" INTEGER NOT NULL,
   108→    "nullable" TEXT,
   109→    PRIMARY KEY ("id")
   110→);
   111→```
   112→
   113→#### INSERT Operations
   114→
   115→```cpp
   116→using namespace sqlgen;
   117→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   118→
   119→const auto insert_query = Insert<TestTable>{};
   120→const auto sql = postgres::to_sql(insert_query);
   121→```
   122→
   123→This generates the following PostgreSQL SQL:
   124→
   125→```sql
   126→COPY "public"."TestTable"("field1", "field2", "id", "nullable") 
   127→FROM STDIN WITH DELIMITER '\t' NULL '\e' QUOTE '\a';
   128→```
   129→
   130→For SQLite, the same operation generates:
   131→
   132→```sql
   133→INSERT INTO "TestTable"("field1", "field2", "id", "nullable") 
   134→VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?);
   135→```
   136→
   137→#### DELETE Operations
   138→
   139→```cpp
   140→using namespace sqlgen;
   141→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   142→
   143→const auto delete_query = delete_from<TestTable> | 
   144→                         where("field2"_c > 0);
   145→const auto sql = postgres::to_sql(delete_query);
   146→```
   147→
   148→This generates the following SQL:
   149→
   150→```sql
   151→DELETE FROM "TestTable" 
   152→WHERE "field2" > 0;
   153→```
   154→
   155→
   156→### Dialect-Specific Features
   157→
   158→Each database dialect implements its own version of `to_sql` with dialect-specific features:
   159→
   160→#### PostgreSQL (`sqlgen::postgres::to_sql`)
   161→
   162→- Uses `COPY` for bulk inserts
   163→- Supports schema names (e.g., "public")
   164→- Uses PostgreSQL-specific escaping rules
   165→
   166→#### SQLite (`sqlgen::sqlite::to_sql`)
   167→
   168→- Uses `INSERT INTO` for inserts
   169→- Uses SQLite-specific escaping rules
   170→- Simpler schema (no schema names)
   171→
   172→## Notes
   173→
   174→- Each dialect's `to_sql` is a template function that works with any sqlgen operation
   175→- The functions are `noexcept` and return a `std::string`
   176→- The generated SQL is properly escaped and safe to use
   177→- The functions are particularly useful for:
   178→  - Debugging complex queries
   179→  - Logging SQL operations
   180→  - Understanding the exact SQL that will be executed
   181→  - Testing and validation
   182→- Each dialect's implementation ensures the generated SQL is compatible with that specific database
   183→- The functions preserve all SQL operations' semantics while adapting to dialect-specific syntax
   184→

1→# `sqlgen::sqlite`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::sqlite` module provides a type-safe and efficient interface for interacting with SQLite databases. It implements the core database operations through a connection-based API with support for prepared statements, transactions, and efficient data iteration.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Connection
     8→
     9→Create a connection to a SQLite database:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→// Connect to an in-memory database
    13→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect();
    14→
    15→// Connect to a file-based database
    16→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
    17→```
    18→
    19→The connection is wrapped in a `sqlgen::Result<Ref<Connection>>` for error handling:
    20→
    21→```cpp
    22→// Handle connection errors
    23→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
    24→if (!conn) {
    25→    // Handle error...
    26→    return;
    27→}
    28→
    29→using namespace sqlgen;
    30→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    31→
    32→const auto query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>> |
    33→                   where("age"_c < 18 and "first_name"_c != "Hugo");
    34→
    35→// Use the connection
    36→const auto minors = query(conn);
    37→```
    38→
    39→## Notes
    40→
    41→- The module provides a type-safe interface for SQLite operations
    42→- All operations return `sqlgen::Result<T>` for error handling
    43→- Prepared statements are used for efficient query execution
    44→- The iterator interface supports batch processing of results
    45→- SQL generation adapts to SQLite's dialect
    46→- The module supports:
    47→  - In-memory and file-based databases
    48→  - Transactions
    49→  - Prepared statements
    50→  - Efficient batch operations
    51→  - Type-safe SQL generation
    52→  - Error handling through `Result<T>`
    53→  - Resource management through `Ref<T>`
    54→

1→# ![C++](https://img.shields.io/badge/c++-%2300599C.svg?style=for-the-badge&logo=c%2B%2B&logoColor=white) sqlgen 
     2→
     3→[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
     4→[![Maintenance](https://img.shields.io/badge/Maintained%3F-yes-green.svg)](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp/graphs/commit-activity)
     5→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/C++-20-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     6→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/gcc-11+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     7→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/clang-14+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     8→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/MSVC-17+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     9→
    10→**📖 Documentation**: [Click here](docs/README.md)
    11→
    12→**sqlgen** is a modern, type-safe ORM and SQL query generator for C++20, inspired by Python's [SQLAlchemy](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy)/[SQLModel](https://github.com/fastapi/sqlmodel) and Rust's [Diesel](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel). It provides a fluent, composable interface for database operations with compile-time type checking and SQL injection protection.
    13→
    14→sqlgen is based on and tightly integrated with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp), a C++-20 library for fast serialization, deserialization and validation using reflection, similar to pydantic in Python, serde in Rust, encoding in Go or aeson in Haskell.
    15→
    16→Together, reflect-cpp and sqlgen enable reliable and efficient ETL pipelines.
    17→
    18→## Features
    19→
    20→- 🔒 **Type Safety**: Compile-time validation of table schemas and queries
    21→- 🛡️ **SQL Injection Protection**: Built-in input validation and parameterized queries
    22→- 🔄 **Composable Queries**: Fluent interface for building complex queries
    23→- 🚀 **High Performance**: Efficient batch operations and prepared statements
    24→- 📦 **Modern C++**: Leverages C++20 features for a clean, expressive API
    25→- 🔌 **Multiple Backends**: Support for PostgreSQL and SQLite
    26→- 🔍 **Reflection Integration**: Seamless integration with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp) 
    27→
    28→## Supported databases 
    29→
    30→The following table lists the databases currently supported by sqlgen and the underlying libraries used:
    31→
    32→| Database      | Library                                                                  | Version      | License       | Remarks                                              |
    33→|---------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------|---------------| -----------------------------------------------------|
    34→| MySQL/MariaDB | [libmariadb](https://github.com/mariadb-corporation/mariadb-connector-c) | >= 3.4.5     | LGPL          |                                                      |
    35→| PostgreSQL    | [libpq](https://github.com/postgres/postgres)                            | >= 16.4      | PostgreSQL    | Will work for all libpq-compatible databases         |
    36→| sqlite        | [sqlite](https://sqlite.org/index.html)                                  | >= 3.49.1    | Public Domain |                                                      |
    37→
    38→## Quick Start
    39→
    40→### Installation using vcpkg
    41→
    42→1. Make sure you have the required dependencies installed (skip this step on Windows):
    43→```bash
    44→sudo apt-get install autoconf bison flex # Linux (Ubuntu, Debian, ...)
    45→brew install autoconf bison flex # macOS
    46→```
    47→
    48→2. Set up vcpkg:
    49→```bash
    50→git submodule update --init
    51→./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.sh  # Linux, macOS
    52→./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.bat # Windows
    53→```
    54→
    55→3. Build the library:
    56→```bash
    57→cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_CXX_STANDARD=20 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
    58→cmake --build build -j 4  # gcc, clang
    59→cmake --build build --config Release -j 4  # MSVC
    60→```
    61→
    62→This will build the static library. To build the shared library 
    63→add `-DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON -DVCPKG_TARGET_TRIPLET=...` to the first line.
    64→Run `./vcpkg/vcpkg help triplets` to view all supported triplets. 
    65→Common triplets for shared libraries are `x64-linux-dynamic`, 
    66→`arm64-osx-dynamic` or `x64-osx-dynamic`.   
    67→
    68→Add `-DSQLGEN_MYSQL=ON` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
    69→
    70→4. Include in your CMake project:
    71→```cmake
    72→find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)
    73→target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
    74→```
    75→
    76→### Installation using Conan
    77→
    78→1. Install Conan (assuming you have Python and pipx installed):
    79→
    80→```bash
    81→pipx install conan
    82→conan profile detect
    83→```
    84→
    85→For older versions of pip, you can also use `pip` instead of `pipx`.
    86→
    87→2. Build the library:
    88→
    89→```bash
    90→conan build . --build=missing -s compiler.cppstd=gnu20
    91→```
    92→
    93→This will build the static library. To build the shared library,
    94→add `-o */*:shared=True`. 
    95→
    96→Add `-o sqlgen/*:with_mysql=True` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
    97→
    98→3. Include in your CMake project:
    99→```cmake
   100→find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)
   101→target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
   102→```
   103→
   104→You can call `conan inspect .` to get an overview of the supported options.
   105→
   106→## Usage Examples
   107→
   108→### Hello World
   109→
   110→```cpp
   111→#include <sqlgen/sqlite.hpp>
   112→#include <iostream>
   113→
   114→struct User {
   115→    std::string name;
   116→    int age;
   117→};
   118→
   119→int main() {
   120→    // Connect to SQLite database
   121→    const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("test.db");
   122→    
   123→    // Create and insert a user
   124→    const auto user = User{.name = "John", .age = 30};
   125→    sqlgen::write(conn, user);
   126→    
   127→    // Read all users
   128→    const auto users = sqlgen::read<std::vector<User>>(conn).value();
   129→    
   130→    for (const auto& u : users) {
   131→        std::cout << u.name << " is " << u.age << " years old\n";
   132→    }
   133→}
   134→```
   135→
   136→### Connecting to a Database
   137→
   138→```cpp
   139→#include <sqlgen/postgres.hpp>
   140→
   141→// PostgreSQL connection
   142→const auto credentials = sqlgen::postgres::Credentials{
   143→    .user = "username",
   144→    .password = "password",
   145→    .host = "localhost",
   146→    .dbname = "mydb",
   147→    .port = 5432
   148→};
   149→
   150→const auto conn = sqlgen::postgres::connect(credentials);
   151→
   152→// SQLite connection
   153→const auto sqlite_conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
   154→```
   155→
   156→### Defining Models
   157→
   158→```cpp
   159→struct Person {
   160→    std::string first_name;
   161→    std::string last_name;
   162→    uint32_t age;
   163→    std::optional<std::string> email;  // Nullable field
   164→};
   165→```
   166→
   167→### Inserting Data
   168→
   169→```cpp
   170→const auto people = std::vector<Person>({
   171→    Person{.first_name = "Homer", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 45},
   172→    Person{.first_name = "Marge", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 42}
   173→});
   174→
   175→// Automatically creates table if it doesn't exist
   176→// (recall that the table is fully defined at compile time)
   177→const auto result = sqlgen::write(conn, people);
   178→
   179→if (!result) {
   180→    std::cerr << "Error: " << result.error().what() << std::endl;
   181→}
   182→```
   183→
   184→Or:
   185→
   186→```cpp
   187→...
   188→
   189→// write(...) abstracts these steps away, but
   190→// if you prefer more granular control, you
   191→// can use sqlgen::insert.
   192→const auto result = begin_transaction(conn)
   193→                        .and_then(create_table<Person> | if_not_exists)
   194→                        .and_then(insert(std::ref(people)))
   195→                        .and_then(commit);
   196→
   197→...
   198→```
   199→
   200→Generated SQL:
   201→```sql
   202→BEGIN TRANSACTION;
   203→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Person" (
   204→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
   205→    "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
   206→    "age" INTEGER NOT NULL,
   207→    "email" TEXT
   208→);
   209→
   210→INSERT INTO "Person" ("first_name", "last_name", "age", "email") 
   211→VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?);
   212→COMMIT;
   213→```
   214→
   215→### Querying Data
   216→
   217→```cpp
   218→#include <rfl/json.hpp>
   219→#include <sqlgen/postgres.hpp>
   220→
   221→using namespace sqlgen;
   222→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   223→
   224→// Build a query for adults, ordered by age
   225→const auto query = read<std::vector<Person>> |
   226→                   where("age"_c >= 18) |
   227→                   order_by("age"_c.desc(), "last_name"_c) |
   228→                   limit(10);
   229→
   230→// Execute the query
   231→const auto result = query(conn);
   232→
   233→if (result) {
   234→    // Print results as JSON
   235→    std::cout << rfl::json::write(*result) << std::endl;
   236→} else {
   237→    std::cerr << "Error: " << result.error().what() << std::endl;
   238→}
   239→```
   240→
   241→Generated SQL:
   242→```sql
   243→SELECT "first_name", "last_name", "age", "email"
   244→FROM "Person"
   245→WHERE "age" >= 18
   246→ORDER BY "age" DESC, "last_name"
   247→LIMIT 10;
   248→```
   249→
   250→### Grouping and Aggregating Data
   251→
   252→```cpp
   253→using namespace sqlgen;
   254→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   255→
   256→struct Children {
   257→    std::string last_name;
   258→    int num_children;
   259→    int max_age;
   260→    int min_age;
   261→    int sum_age;
   262→};
   263→
   264→const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
   265→    "last_name"_c,
   266→    count().as<"num_children">(),
   267→    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),
   268→    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),
   269→    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),
   270→) | where("age"_c < 18) | group_by("last_name"_c) | to<std::vector<Children>>;
   271→
   272→const std::vector<Children> children = get_children(conn).value();
   273→```
   274→
   275→Generated SQL:
   276→```sql
   277→SELECT 
   278→    "last_name",
   279→    COUNT(*) as "num_children",
   280→    MAX("age") as "max_age",
   281→    MIN("age") as "min_age",
   282→    SUM("age") as "sum_age"
   283→FROM "Person"
   284→WHERE "age" < 18
   285→GROUP BY "last_name";
   286→```
   287→
   288→### Joining data
   289→
   290→```cpp
   291→using namespace sqlgen;
   292→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   293→
   294→struct ParentAndChild {
   295→    std::string last_name;
   296→    std::string first_name_parent;
   297→    std::string first_name_child;
   298→    double parent_age_at_birth;
   299→};
   300→
   301→const auto get_people =
   302→  select_from<Person, "t1">(
   303→      "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,

   429→### Type Safety and SQL Injection Protection
   430→
   431→sqlgen provides comprehensive compile-time checks and runtime protection:
   432→
   433→```cpp
   434→// Compile-time error: No such column "color"
   435→const auto query = read<std::vector<Person>> |
   436→                   where("color"_c == "blue");
   437→
   438→// Compile-time error: Cannot compare column "age" to a string 
   439→const auto query = read<std::vector<Person>> |
   440→                   where("age"_c == "Homer");
   441→
   442→// Compile-time error: "age" must be aggregated or included in GROUP BY 
   443→const auto query = select_from<Person>(
   444→    "last_name"_c,
   445→    "age"_c 
   446→) | group_by("last_name"_c);
   447→
   448→// Compile-time error: Cannot add string and int 
   449→const auto query = select_from<Person>(
   450→    "last_name"_c + "age"_c 
   451→);
   452→
   453→// Runtime protection against SQL injection
   454→std::vector<Person> get_people(const auto& conn, 
   455→                              const sqlgen::AlphaNumeric& first_name) {
   456→    using namespace sqlgen;
   457→    return (read<std::vector<Person>> | 
   458→            where("first_name"_c == first_name))(conn).value();
   459→}
   460→
   461→// This will be rejected
   462→get_people(conn, "Homer' OR '1'='1");  // SQL injection attempt
   463→```

1→# `sqlgen::inner_join`, `sqlgen::left_join`, `sqlgen::right_join`, `sqlgen::full_join`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen` library provides a type-safe, composable interface for expressing SQL joins in C++. It supports all standard SQL join types (inner, left, right, full) and allows for both simple and nested join queries, including joining on subqueries.
     4→
     5→## Join Types
     6→
     7→The following join types are available:
     8→
     9→- `inner_join` — Returns rows when there is a match in both tables
    10→- `left_join` — Returns all rows from the left table, and matched rows from the right table
    11→- `right_join` — Returns all rows from the right table, and matched rows from the left table
    12→- `full_join` — Returns all rows when there is a match in one of the tables (not supported by MariaDB)
    13→
    14→Each join type can be used with either a table or a subquery, and can be aliased for use in complex queries.
    15→
    16→## Usage
    17→
    18→### Basic Join Example
    19→
    20→```cpp
    21→using namespace sqlgen;
    22→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    23→
    24→struct Person {
    25→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id;
    26→    std::string first_name;
    27→    std::string last_name;
    28→    double age;
    29→};
    30→
    31→struct Relationship {
    32→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> parent_id;
    33→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> child_id;
    34→};
    35→
    36→// Join two tables: Relationship (as t1) and Person (as t2)
    37→const auto get_children =
    38→    select_from<Relationship, "t1">(
    39→        "parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
    40→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
    41→        "age"_t2 | as<"age">
    42→    ) |
    43→    left_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
    44→```
    45→
    46→This produces a query equivalent to:
    47→
    48→```sql
    49→SELECT t1."parent_id" AS "id", t2."first_name" AS "first_name", t2."age" AS "age"
    50→FROM "Relationship" t1
    51→LEFT JOIN "Person" t2 ON t2."id" = t1."child_id"
    52→```
    53→
    54→### Chaining Multiple Joins
    55→
    56→You can chain multiple joins to build more complex queries:
    57→
    58→```cpp
    59→const auto get_people =
    60→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
    61→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
    62→        "first_name"_t3 | as<"first_name_child">,
    63→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t3) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
    64→    ) |
    65→    inner_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2) |
    66→    left_join<Person, "t3">("id"_t3 == "child_id"_t2) |
    67→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t3) |
    68→    order_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t3) |
    69→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
    70→```
    71→
    72→This produces a query with both an inner and a left join, grouping and ordering the results.
    73→
    74→### Nested Joins and Subqueries
    75→
    76→`sqlgen` allows you to join on subqueries, enabling nested join patterns:
    77→
    78→```cpp
    79→const auto get_children =
    80→    select_from<Relationship, "t1">(
    81→        "parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
    82→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
    83→        "age"_t2 | as<"age">
    84→    ) |
    85→    left_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
    86→
    87→const auto get_people =
    88→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
    89→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
    90→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
    91→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
    92→    ) |
    93→    inner_join<"t2">(get_children, "id"_t1 == "id"_t2) |
    94→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t2) |
    95→    order_by("first_name"_t2) |
    96→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
    97→```
    98→
    99→This produces a query with a subquery in the join clause:
   100→
   101→```sql
   102→SELECT t1."last_name" AS "last_name", t2."first_name" AS "first_name_child", AVG((t1."age") - (t2."age")) AS "avg_parent_age_at_birth"
   103→FROM "Person" t1
   104→INNER JOIN (
   105→    SELECT t1."parent_id" AS "id", t2."first_name" AS "first_name", t2."age" AS "age"
   106→    FROM "Relationship" t1
   107→    INNER JOIN "Person" t2 ON t2."id" = t1."child_id"
   108→) t2 ON t1."id" = t2."id"
   109→GROUP BY t1."last_name", t2."first_name"
   110→ORDER BY t2."first_name"
   111→```
   112→
   113→## Join Syntax
   114→
   115→- `inner_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Inner join with a table
   116→- `left_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Left join with a table
   117→- `right_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Right join with a table
   118→- `full_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Full join with a table
   119→- `inner_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Inner join with a subquery
   120→- `left_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Left join with a subquery
   121→- `right_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Right join with a subquery
   122→- `full_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Full join with a subquery
   123→
   124→Where:
   125→- `Table` is the C++ struct representing the table
   126→- `Alias` is a string literal alias for the table or subquery
   127→- `condition` is a boolean expression relating columns from the joined tables
   128→- `subquery` is a previously constructed query expression
   129→
   130→## Aliasing and Column References
   131→
   132→When joining tables or subqueries, you must use aliases to disambiguate columns. Use the `_t1`, `_t2`, etc. 
   133→suffixes to refer to columns from different tables or subqueries, which are defined in the 
   134→namespace `sqlgen::literals`:
   135→
   136→```cpp
   137→"id"_t1, "first_name"_t2, "age"_t3
   138→```
   139→
   140→The library includes predefined suffixes from `_t1` to `_t99`.
   141→
   142→If you want to use your own alias, you can use this syntax instead:
   143→
   144→```cpp
   145→col<"id", "your_alias">, col<"first_name", "your_alias">, col<"age", "your_alias">
   146→```
   147→
   148→## Advanced: Nested and Grouped Joins
   149→
   150→You can nest joins and combine them with grouping and aggregation:
   151→
   152→```cpp
   153→const auto get_people =
   154→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   155→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   156→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
   157→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
   158→    ) |
   159→    inner_join<"t2">(get_children, "id"_t1 == "id"_t2) |
   160→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t2) |
   161→    order_by("first_name"_t2) |
   162→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   163→```
   164→
   165→## Nullability in Joins
   166→
   167→When performing outer joins (`left_join`, `right_join`, `full_join`), columns from the joined table may contain `NULL` values if no matching row is found. `sqlgen` handles this by wrapping the type of such columns in `std::optional`. If a field is already nullable (i.e., `std::optional<T>`), it remains `std::optional<T>`.
   168→
   169→-   `inner_join`: Does not introduce nullability. The types of the selected columns remain unchanged.
   170→-   `left_join`: Columns selected from the right table (the one being joined) will become `std::optional<T>` if they are not already nullable.
   171→-   `right_join`: Columns selected from the left table (the `select_from` table) will become `std::optional<T>` if they are not already nullable.
   172→-   `full_join`: Columns selected from both tables will become `std::optional<T>` if they are not already nullable.
   173→
   174→### Example: Nullability in a `left_join`
   175→
   176→Consider a `left_join` between `Person` and `Relationship` tables. If a person has no corresponding relationship, the columns from `Relationship` will be `NULL`.
   177→
   178→```cpp
   179→struct PersonWithOptionalRelationship {
   180→    uint32_t id;
   181→    std::string first_name;
   182→    std::optional<uint32_t> child_id;
   183→};
   184→
   185→const auto get_people_with_optional_relationship =
   186→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   187→        "id"_t1 | as<"id">,
   188→        "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name">,
   189→        "child_id"_t2 | as<"child_id">
   190→    ) |
   191→    left_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2) |
   192→    to<std::vector<PersonWithOptionalRelationship>>;
   193→```
   194→
   195→In this example, `child_id` is selected from the right table (`Relationship`) of a `left_join`. Therefore, its type in the result struct `PersonWithOptionalRelationship` must be `std::optional<uint32_t>` to handle cases where no matching relationship is found.
   196→
   197→### Nullability in Multi-Table Joins
   198→
   199→Nullability propagates through chained joins. If a table becomes nullable due to an outer join, any subsequent joins that use columns from that table will also treat them as nullable.
   200→
   201→For example, consider a query that joins `Person` to `Relationship` (left join) and then `Relationship` to a hypothetical `Pet` table (left join).
   202→
   203→```cpp
   204→struct PersonWithPets {
   205→    uint32_t person_id;
   206→    std::optional<uint32_t> child_id;
   207→    std::optional<std::string> pet_name;
   208→};
   209→
   210→// Assume Pet table has { id, name, owner_id }
   211→const auto get_people_with_pets =
   212→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   213→        "id"_t1 | as<"person_id">,
   214→        "child_id"_t2 | as<"child_id">,
   215→        "name"_t3 | as<"pet_name">
   216→    ) |
   217→    left_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2) |
   218→    left_join<Pet, "t3">("child_id"_t2 == "owner_id"_t3) | // Joining on a nullable-prone column
   219→    to<std::vector<PersonWithPets>>;
   220→```
   221→
   222→In this query:
   223→1.  The first `left_join` makes columns from `Relationship` (`t2`) nullable. So, `child_id` becomes `std::optional<uint32_t>`.
   224→2.  The second `left_join` joins `Pet` (`t3`). Since `t3` is on the right side of a `left_join`, its columns (like `pet_name`) also become nullable, resulting in `std::optional<std::string>`.
   225→
   226→If an `inner_join` were used for the second join (`Pet`), `pet_name` would still be `std::optional<std::string>` if the `Pet` table itself has a nullable `name` column. However, the join logic itself wouldn't introduce nullability for the `Pet` table's columns. The key principle is that the nullability of a column in the final result depends on both its original type and the types of joins applied to its table.
   227→
   228→## Notes
   229→
   230→- Joins can be chained and nested arbitrarily
   231→- Aliases are required for all joined tables and subqueries
   232→- Join conditions must use the correct aliases for columns
   233→- You can join on subqueries, enabling powerful query composition
   234→- Joins can be combined with `group_by`, `order_by`, and aggregation functions
   235→- The result type must match the structure of your select statement, with field names matching the aliases used in the query
   236→
   237→## Example: Full Nested Join Query
   238→
   239→```cpp
   240→struct ParentAndChild {
   241→    std::string last_name;
   242→    std::string first_name_child;
   243→    double avg_parent_age_at_birth;
   244→};
   245→
   246→const auto get_children =
   247→    select_from<Relationship, "t1">("parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
   248→                                    "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
   249→                                    "age"_t2 | as<"age">) |
   250→    inner_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
   251→
   252→const auto get_people =
   253→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   254→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   255→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
   256→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
   257→    ) |
   258→    inner_join<"t2">(get_children, "id"_t1 == "id"_t2) |
   259→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t2) |
   260→    order_by("first_name"_t2) |
   261→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   262→```
   263→
   264→This query joins a table to a subquery, groups by two columns, and computes an aggregate over the join.
   265→

1→# `sqlgen::inner_join`, `sqlgen::left_join`, `sqlgen::right_join`, `sqlgen::full_join`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen` library provides a type-safe, composable interface for expressing SQL joins in C++. It supports all standard SQL join types (inner, left, right, full) and allows for both simple and nested join queries, including joining on subqueries.
     4→
     5→## Join Types
     6→
     7→The following join types are available:
     8→
     9→- `inner_join` — Returns rows when there is a match in both tables
    10→- `left_join` — Returns all rows from the left table, and matched rows from the right table
    11→- `right_join` — Returns all rows from the right table, and matched rows from the left table
    12→- `full_join` — Returns all rows when there is a match in one of the tables (not supported by MariaDB)
    13→
    14→Each join type can be used with either a table or a subquery, and can be aliased for use in complex queries.
    15→
    16→## Usage
    17→
    18→### Basic Join Example
    19→
    20→```cpp
    21→using namespace sqlgen;
    22→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    23→
    24→struct Person {
    25→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id;
    26→    std::string first_name;
    27→    std::string last_name;
    28→    double age;
    29→};
    30→
    31→struct Relationship {
    32→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> parent_id;
    33→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> child_id;
    34→};
    35→
    36→// Join two tables: Relationship (as t1) and Person (as t2)
    37→const auto get_children =
    38→    select_from<Relationship, "t1">(
    39→        "parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
    40→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
    41→        "age"_t2 | as<"age">
    42→    ) |
    43→    left_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
    44→```
    45→
    46→This produces a query equivalent to:
    47→
    48→```sql
    49→SELECT t1."parent_id" AS "id", t2."first_name" AS "first_name", t2."age" AS "age"
    50→FROM "Relationship" t1
    51→LEFT JOIN "Person" t2 ON t2."id" = t1."child_id"
    52→```
    53→
    54→### Chaining Multiple Joins
    55→
    56→You can chain multiple joins to build more complex queries:
    57→
    58→```cpp
    59→const auto get_people =
    60→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
    61→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
    62→        "first_name"_t3 | as<"first_name_child">,
    63→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t3) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
    64→    ) |
    65→    inner_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2) |
    66→    left_join<Person, "t3">("id"_t3 == "child_id"_t2) |
    67→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t3) |
    68→    order_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t3) |
    69→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
    70→```
    71→
    72→This produces a query with both an inner and a left join, grouping and ordering the results.
    73→
    74→### Nested Joins and Subqueries
    75→
    76→`sqlgen` allows you to join on subqueries, enabling nested join patterns:
    77→
    78→```cpp
    79→const auto get_children =
    80→    select_from<Relationship, "t1">(
    81→        "parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
    82→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
    83→        "age"_t2 | as<"age">
    84→    ) |
    85→    left_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
    86→
    87→const auto get_people =
    88→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
    89→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
    90→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
    91→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
    92→    ) |
    93→    inner_join<"t2">(get_children, "id"_t1 == "id"_t2) |
    94→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t2) |
    95→    order_by("first_name"_t2) |
    96→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
    97→```
    98→
    99→This produces a query with a subquery in the join clause:
   100→
   101→```sql
   102→SELECT t1."last_name" AS "last_name", t2."first_name" AS "first_name_child", AVG((t1."age") - (t2."age")) AS "avg_parent_age_at_birth"
   103→FROM "Person" t1
   104→INNER JOIN (
   105→    SELECT t1."parent_id" AS "id", t2."first_name" AS "first_name", t2."age" AS "age"
   106→    FROM "Relationship" t1
   107→    INNER JOIN "Person" t2 ON t2."id" = t1."child_id"
   108→) t2 ON t1."id" = t2."id"
   109→GROUP BY t1."last_name", t2."first_name"
   110→ORDER BY t2."first_name"
   111→```
   112→
   113→## Join Syntax
   114→
   115→- `inner_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Inner join with a table
   116→- `left_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Left join with a table
   117→- `right_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Right join with a table
   118→- `full_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Full join with a table
   119→- `inner_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Inner join with a subquery
   120→- `left_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Left join with a subquery
   121→- `right_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Right join with a subquery
   122→- `full_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Full join with a subquery
   123→
   124→Where:
   125→- `Table` is the C++ struct representing the table
   126→- `Alias` is a string literal alias for the table or subquery
   127→- `condition` is a boolean expression relating columns from the joined tables
   128→- `subquery` is a previously constructed query expression
   129→
   130→## Aliasing and Column References
   131→
   132→When joining tables or subqueries, you must use aliases to disambiguate columns. Use the `_t1`, `_t2`, etc. 
   133→suffixes to refer to columns from different tables or subqueries, which are defined in the 
   134→namespace `sqlgen::literals`:
   135→
   136→```cpp
   137→"id"_t1, "first_name"_t2, "age"_t3
   138→```
   139→
   140→The library includes predefined suffixes from `_t1` to `_t99`.
   141→
   142→If you want to use your own alias, you can use this syntax instead:
   143→
   144→```cpp
   145→col<"id", "your_alias">, col<"first_name", "your_alias">, col<"age", "your_alias">
   146→```
   147→
   148→## Advanced: Nested and Grouped Joins
   149→
   150→You can nest joins and combine them with grouping and aggregation:
   151→
   152→```cpp
   153→const auto get_people =
   154→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   155→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   156→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
   157→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
   158→    ) |
   159→    inner_join<"t2">(get_children, "id"_t1 == "id"_t2) |
   160→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t2) |
   161→    order_by("first_name"_t2) |
   162→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   163→```
   164→
   165→## Nullability in Joins
   166→
   167→When performing outer joins (`left_join`, `right_join`, `full_join`), columns from the joined table may contain `NULL` values if no matching row is found. `sqlgen` handles this by wrapping the type of such columns in `std::optional`. If a field is already nullable (i.e., `std::optional<T>`), it remains `std::optional<T>`.
   168→
   169→-   `inner_join`: Does not introduce nullability. The types of the selected columns remain unchanged.
   170→-   `left_join`: Columns selected from the right table (the one being joined) will become `std::optional<T>` if they are not already nullable.
   171→-   `right_join`: Columns selected from the left table (the `select_from` table) will become `std::optional<T>` if they are not already nullable.
   172→-   `full_join`: Columns selected from both tables will become `std::optional<T>` if they are not already nullable.
   173→
   174→### Example: Nullability in a `left_join`
   175→
   176→Consider a `left_join` between `Person` and `Relationship` tables. If a person has no corresponding relationship, the columns from `Relationship` will be `NULL`.
   177→
   178→```cpp
   179→struct PersonWithOptionalRelationship {
   180→    uint32_t id;
   181→    std::string first_name;
   182→    std::optional<uint32_t> child_id;
   183→};
   184→
   185→const auto get_people_with_optional_relationship =
   186→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   187→        "id"_t1 | as<"id">,
   188→        "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name">,
   189→        "child_id"_t2 | as<"child_id">
   190→    ) |
   191→    left_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2) |
   192→    to<std::vector<PersonWithOptionalRelationship>>;
   193→```
   194→
   195→In this example, `child_id` is selected from the right table (`Relationship`) of a `left_join`. Therefore, its type in the result struct `PersonWithOptionalRelationship` must be `std::optional<uint32_t>` to handle cases where no matching relationship is found.
   196→
   197→### Nullability in Multi-Table Joins
   198→
   199→Nullability propagates through chained joins. If a table becomes nullable due to an outer join, any subsequent joins that use columns from that table will also treat them as nullable.
   200→
   201→For example, consider a query that joins `Person` to `Relationship` (left join) and then `Relationship` to a hypothetical `Pet` table (left join).
   202→
   203→```cpp
   204→struct PersonWithPets {
   205→    uint32_t person_id;
   206→    std::optional<uint32_t> child_id;
   207→    std::optional<std::string> pet_name;
   208→};
   209→
   210→// Assume Pet table has { id, name, owner_id }
   211→const auto get_people_with_pets =
   212→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   213→        "id"_t1 | as<"person_id">,
   214→        "child_id"_t2 | as<"child_id">,
   215→        "name"_t3 | as<"pet_name">
   216→    ) |
   217→    left_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2) |
   218→    left_join<Pet, "t3">("child_id"_t2 == "owner_id"_t3) | // Joining on a nullable-prone column
   219→    to<std::vector<PersonWithPets>>;
   220→```
   221→
   222→In this query:
   223→1.  The first `left_join` makes columns from `Relationship` (`t2`) nullable. So, `child_id` becomes `std::optional<uint32_t>`.
   224→2.  The second `left_join` joins `Pet` (`t3`). Since `t3` is on the right side of a `left_join`, its columns (like `pet_name`) also become nullable, resulting in `std::optional<std::string>`.
   225→
   226→If an `inner_join` were used for the second join (`Pet`), `pet_name` would still be `std::optional<std::string>` if the `Pet` table itself has a nullable `name` column. However, the join logic itself wouldn't introduce nullability for the `Pet` table's columns. The key principle is that the nullability of a column in the final result depends on both its original type and the types of joins applied to its table.
   227→
   228→## Notes
   229→
   230→- Joins can be chained and nested arbitrarily
   231→- Aliases are required for all joined tables and subqueries
   232→- Join conditions must use the correct aliases for columns
   233→- You can join on subqueries, enabling powerful query composition
   234→- Joins can be combined with `group_by`, `order_by`, and aggregation functions
   235→- The result type must match the structure of your select statement, with field names matching the aliases used in the query
   236→
   237→## Example: Full Nested Join Query
   238→
   239→```cpp
   240→struct ParentAndChild {
   241→    std::string last_name;
   242→    std::string first_name_child;
   243→    double avg_parent_age_at_birth;
   244→};
   245→
   246→const auto get_children =
   247→    select_from<Relationship, "t1">("parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
   248→                                    "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
   249→                                    "age"_t2 | as<"age">) |
   250→    inner_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
   251→
   252→const auto get_people =
   253→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   254→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   255→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
   256→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
   257→    ) |
   258→    inner_join<"t2">(get_children, "id"_t1 == "id"_t2) |
   259→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t2) |
   260→    order_by("first_name"_t2) |
   261→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   262→```
   263→
   264→This query joins a table to a subquery, groups by two columns, and computes an aggregate over the join.
   265→

1→# `sqlgen::read` 
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::read` interface provides a flexible and type-safe way to query data from a SQL database into C++ containers or ranges. It supports composable query building with `where`, `order_by`, and `limit` clauses.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Read
     8→
     9→Read all rows from a table into a container (e.g., `std::vector<Person>`):
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
    13→
    14→const std::vector<Person> people = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>>(conn).value();
    15→```
    16→
    17→This generates the following SQL:
    18→
    19→```sql
    20→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age"
    21→FROM "Person";
    22→```
    23→
    24→Note that `conn` is actually a connection wrapped into an `sqlgen::Result<...>`.
    25→This means you can use monadic error handling and fit this into a single line:
    26→
    27→```cpp
    28→// sqlgen::Result<std::vector<Person>>
    29→const auto people = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db").and_then(
    30→                        sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>>);
    31→```
    32→
    33→Please refer to the documentation on `sqlgen::Result<...>` for more information on error handling.
    34→
    35→### With `where` clause
    36→
    37→Filter results using a `where` clause:
    38→
    39→```cpp
    40→using namespace sqlgen;
    41→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    42→
    43→const auto query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>> |
    44→                   where("age"_c < 18 and "first_name"_c != "Hugo");
    45→
    46→const auto minors = query(conn).value();
    47→```
    48→
    49→This generates the following SQL:
    50→
    51→```sql
    52→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age"
    53→FROM "Person"
    54→WHERE 
    55→    ("age" < 18) AND 
    56→    ("first_name" != 'Hugo');
    57→```
    58→
    59→Note that `"..."_c` refers to the name of the column. If such a field does not
    60→exists on the struct `Person`, the code will fail to compile. It is defined in 
    61→the namespace `sqlgen::literals`.
    62→
    63→You can also use monadic error handling here:
    64→
    65→```cpp
    66→using namespace sqlgen;
    67→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    68→
    69→const auto query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>> |
    70→                   where("age"_c < 18 and "first_name"_c != "Hugo");
    71→
    72→// sqlgen::Result<std::vector<Person>>
    73→const auto minors = sqlite::connect("database.db").and_then(query);
    74→```
    75→
    76→### With `order_by` and `limit`
    77→
    78→Sort and limit results:
    79→
    80→```cpp
    81→using namespace sqlgen;
    82→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    83→
    84→const auto query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>> |
    85→                   order_by("age"_c) |
    86→                   limit(2);
    87→
    88→const auto youngest_two = query(conn).value();
    89→```
    90→
    91→This generates the following SQL:
    92→
    93→```sql
    94→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age"
    95→FROM "Person"
    96→ORDER BY "age"
    97→LIMIT 2;
    98→```
    99→
   100→### With ranges
   101→
   102→Read results as a lazy range:
   103→
   104→```cpp
   105→const auto people_range = sqlgen::read<sqlgen::Range<Person>>(conn).value();
   106→
   107→for (const sqlgen::Result<Person>& person : people_range) {
   108→    // process result 
   109→}
   110→```
   111→
   112→`people_range` satisfies the `std::ranges::input_range` concept, making it compatible with C++20 ranges and views. This allows for memory-efficient iteration through database results and enables composition with other range operations:
   113→
   114→```cpp
   115→using namespace std::ranges::views;
   116→
   117→// Transform range results
   118→const auto first_names = people_range | transform([](const sqlgen::Result<Person>& r) {
   119→    return r.value().first_name;
   120→});
   121→
   122→// Filter range results
   123→const auto adults = people_range | filter([](const sqlgen::Result<Person>& r) {
   124→    return r && r->age >= 18;
   125→});
   126→```
   127→
   128→## Example: Full Query Composition
   129→
   130→```cpp
   131→using namespace sqlgen;
   132→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   133→
   134→const auto query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>> |
   135→                   where("age"_c >= 18) |
   136→                   order_by("last_name"_c, "first_name"_c.desc()) |
   137→                   limit(10);
   138→
   139→const auto adults = query(conn).value();
   140→```
   141→
   142→This generates the following SQL:
   143→
   144→```sql
   145→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age"
   146→FROM "Person"
   147→WHERE 
   148→    ("age" >= 18)
   149→ORDER BY 
   150→    "last_name",
   151→    "first_name" DESC
   152→LIMIT 10;
   153→```
   154→
   155→It is strongly recommended that you use `using namespace sqlgen` and `using namespace sqlgen::literals;`. However,
   156→if you do not want to do that, you can rewrite the example above as follows:
   157→
   158→```cpp
   159→const auto query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>> |
   160→                   sqlgen::where(sqlgen::col<"age"> >= 18) |
   161→                   sqlgen::order_by(sqlgen::col<"last_name">, sqlgen::col<"first_name">.desc()) |
   162→                   sqlgen::limit(10);
   163→
   164→const auto adults = query(conn).value();
   165→```
   166→
   167→## Notes
   168→
   169→- All query clauses (`where`, `order_by`, `limit`) are optional.
   170→- The `Result<ContainerType>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw a exception if the results) or handle errors as needed. Refer to the 
   171→- The `sqlgen::Range<T>` type allows for lazy iteration over results.
   172→- `"..."_c` refers to the name of the column.
   173→

1→# `sqlgen::sqlite`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::sqlite` module provides a type-safe and efficient interface for interacting with SQLite databases. It implements the core database operations through a connection-based API with support for prepared statements, transactions, and efficient data iteration.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Connection
     8→
     9→Create a connection to a SQLite database:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→// Connect to an in-memory database
    13→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect();
    14→
    15→// Connect to a file-based database
    16→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
    17→```
    18→
    19→The connection is wrapped in a `sqlgen::Result<Ref<Connection>>` for error handling:
    20→
    21→```cpp
    22→// Handle connection errors
    23→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
    24→if (!conn) {
    25→    // Handle error...
    26→    return;
    27→}
    28→
    29→using namespace sqlgen;
    30→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    31→
    32→const auto query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>> |
    33→                   where("age"_c < 18 and "first_name"_c != "Hugo");
    34→
    35→// Use the connection
    36→const auto minors = query(conn);
    37→```
    38→
    39→## Notes
    40→
    41→- The module provides a type-safe interface for SQLite operations
    42→- All operations return `sqlgen::Result<T>` for error handling
    43→- Prepared statements are used for efficient query execution
    44→- The iterator interface supports batch processing of results
    45→- SQL generation adapts to SQLite's dialect
    46→- The module supports:
    47→  - In-memory and file-based databases
    48→  - Transactions
    49→  - Prepared statements
    50→  - Efficient batch operations
    51→  - Type-safe SQL generation
    52→  - Error handling through `Result<T>`
    53→  - Resource management through `Ref<T>`
