1→# ![C++](https://img.shields.io/badge/c++-%2300599C.svg?style=for-the-badge&logo=c%2B%2B&logoColor=white) sqlgen 
     2→
     3→[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
     4→[![Maintenance](https://img.shields.io/badge/Maintained%3F-yes-green.svg)](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp/graphs/commit-activity)
     5→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/C++-20-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     6→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/gcc-11+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     7→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/clang-14+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     8→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/MSVC-17+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     9→
    10→**📖 Documentation**: [Click here](docs/README.md)
    11→
    12→**sqlgen** is a modern, type-safe ORM and SQL query generator for C++20, inspired by Python's [SQLAlchemy](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy)/[SQLModel](https://github.com/fastapi/sqlmodel) and Rust's [Diesel](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel). It provides a fluent, composable interface for database operations with compile-time type checking and SQL injection protection.
    13→
    14→sqlgen is based on and tightly integrated with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp), a C++-20 library for fast serialization, deserialization and validation using reflection, similar to pydantic in Python, serde in Rust, encoding in Go or aeson in Haskell.
    15→
    16→Together, reflect-cpp and sqlgen enable reliable and efficient ETL pipelines.
    17→
    18→## Features
    19→
    20→- 🔒 **Type Safety**: Compile-time validation of table schemas and queries
    21→- 🛡️ **SQL Injection Protection**: Built-in input validation and parameterized queries
    22→- 🔄 **Composable Queries**: Fluent interface for building complex queries
    23→- 🚀 **High Performance**: Efficient batch operations and prepared statements
    24→- 📦 **Modern C++**: Leverages C++20 features for a clean, expressive API
    25→- 🔌 **Multiple Backends**: Support for PostgreSQL and SQLite
    26→- 🔍 **Reflection Integration**: Seamless integration with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp) 
    27→
    28→## Supported databases 
    29→
    30→The following table lists the databases currently supported by sqlgen and the underlying libraries used:
    31→
    32→| Database      | Library                                                                  | Version      | License       | Remarks                                              |
    33→|---------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------|---------------| -----------------------------------------------------|
    34→| MySQL/MariaDB | [libmariadb](https://github.com/mariadb-corporation/mariadb-connector-c) | >= 3.4.5     | LGPL          |                                                      |
    35→| PostgreSQL    | [libpq](https://github.com/postgres/postgres)                            | >= 16.4      | PostgreSQL    | Will work for all libpq-compatible databases         |
    36→| sqlite        | [sqlite](https://sqlite.org/index.html)                                  | >= 3.49.1    | Public Domain |                                                      |
    37→
    38→## Quick Start
    39→
    40→### Installation using vcpkg
    41→
    42→1. Make sure you have the required dependencies installed (skip this step on Windows):
    43→```bash
    44→sudo apt-get install autoconf bison flex # Linux (Ubuntu, Debian, ...)
    45→brew install autoconf bison flex # macOS
    46→```
    47→
    48→2. Set up vcpkg:
    49→```bash
    50→git submodule update --init
    51→./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.sh  # Linux, macOS
    52→./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.bat # Windows
    53→```
    54→
    55→3. Build the library:
    56→```bash
    57→cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_CXX_STANDARD=20 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
    58→cmake --build build -j 4  # gcc, clang
    59→cmake --build build --config Release -j 4  # MSVC
    60→```
    61→
    62→This will build the static library. To build the shared library 
    63→add `-DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON -DVCPKG_TARGET_TRIPLET=...` to the first line.
    64→Run `./vcpkg/vcpkg help triplets` to view all supported triplets. 
    65→Common triplets for shared libraries are `x64-linux-dynamic`, 
    66→`arm64-osx-dynamic` or `x64-osx-dynamic`.   
    67→
    68→Add `-DSQLGEN_MYSQL=ON` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
    69→
    70→4. Include in your CMake project:
    71→```cmake
    72→find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)
    73→target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
    74→```
    75→
    76→### Installation using Conan
    77→
    78→1. Install Conan (assuming you have Python and pipx installed):
    79→
    80→```bash
    81→pipx install conan
    82→conan profile detect
    83→```
    84→
    85→For older versions of pip, you can also use `pip` instead of `pipx`.
    86→
    87→2. Build the library:
    88→
    89→```bash
    90→conan build . --build=missing -s compiler.cppstd=gnu20
    91→```
    92→
    93→This will build the static library. To build the shared library,
    94→add `-o */*:shared=True`. 
    95→
    96→Add `-o sqlgen/*:with_mysql=True` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
    97→
    98→3. Include in your CMake project:
    99→```cmake
   100→find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)
   101→target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
   102→```
   103→
   104→You can call `conan inspect .` to get an overview of the supported options.
   105→
   106→## Usage Examples
   107→
   108→### Hello World
   109→
   110→```cpp
   111→#include <sqlgen/sqlite.hpp>
   112→#include <iostream>
   113→
   114→struct User {
   115→    std::string name;
   116→    int age;
   117→};
   118→
   119→int main() {
   120→    // Connect to SQLite database
   121→    const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("test.db");
   122→    
   123→    // Create and insert a user
   124→    const auto user = User{.name = "John", .age = 30};
   125→    sqlgen::write(conn, user);
   126→    
   127→    // Read all users
   128→    const auto users = sqlgen::read<std::vector<User>>(conn).value();
   129→    
   130→    for (const auto& u : users) {
   131→        std::cout << u.name << " is " << u.age << " years old\n";
   132→    }
   133→}
   134→```
   135→
   136→### Connecting to a Database
   137→
   138→```cpp
   139→#include <sqlgen/postgres.hpp>
   140→
   141→// PostgreSQL connection
   142→const auto credentials = sqlgen::postgres::Credentials{
   143→    .user = "username",
   144→    .password = "password",
   145→    .host = "localhost",
   146→    .dbname = "mydb",
   147→    .port = 5432
   148→};
   149→
   150→const auto conn = sqlgen::postgres::connect(credentials);

1→# `sqlgen::col`
     2→
     3→`sqlgen::col` provides a type-safe way to reference and manipulate database columns in SQL queries. It enables building complex SQL conditions, ordering, and updates through a fluent C++ interface.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Definition
     8→
     9→Reference a column using the string literal operator:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→using namespace sqlgen;
    13→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    14→
    15→// Using string literal operator
    16→const auto age_col = "age"_c;
    17→
    18→// Using col template function
    19→const auto name_col = col<"first_name">;
    20→```
    21→
    22→### Column Operations
    23→
    24→#### Comparison Operations
    25→
    26→Compare columns with values or other columns:
    27→
    28→```cpp
    29→using namespace sqlgen;
    30→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    31→
    32→// Compare with value
    33→const auto query1 = read<std::vector<Person>> | where("age"_c > 18);
    34→
    35→// Compare with another column
    36→const auto query2 = read<std::vector<Person>> | 
    37→                   where("age"_c > "id"_c);
    38→```
    39→
    40→This generates SQL like:
    41→
    42→```sql
    43→-- For query1
    44→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age" 
    45→FROM "Person" 
    46→WHERE "age" > 18;
    47→
    48→-- For query2
    49→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age" 
    50→FROM "Person" 
    51→WHERE "age" > "id";
    52→```
    53→
    54→#### NULL Operations
    55→
    56→Check for NULL or NOT NULL values:
    57→
    58→```cpp
    59→using namespace sqlgen;
    60→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    61→
    62→// Find records where age is NULL
    63→const auto query1 = read<std::vector<Person>> | 
    64→                   where("age"_c.is_null());
    65→
    66→// Find records where age is NOT NULL
    67→const auto query2 = read<std::vector<Person>> | 
    68→                   where("age"_c.is_not_null());
    69→```
    70→
    71→This generates SQL like:
    72→
    73→```sql
    74→-- For query1
    75→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age" 
    76→FROM "Person" 
    77→WHERE "age" IS NULL;
    78→
    79→-- For query2
    80→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age" 
    81→FROM "Person" 
    82→WHERE "age" IS NOT NULL;
    83→```
    84→
    85→#### Pattern Matching
    86→
    87→Use LIKE and NOT LIKE for pattern matching:
    88→
    89→```cpp
    90→using namespace sqlgen;
    91→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    92→
    93→// Find names starting with 'H'
    94→const auto query1 = read<std::vector<Person>> | 
    95→                   where("first_name"_c.like("H%"));
    96→
    97→// Find names not starting with 'H'
    98→const auto query2 = read<std::vector<Person>> | 
    99→                   where("first_name"_c.not_like("H%"));
   100→```
   101→
   102→This generates SQL like:
   103→
   104→```sql
   105→-- For query1
   106→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age" 
   107→FROM "Person" 
   108→WHERE "first_name" LIKE 'H%';
   109→
   110→-- For query2
   111→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age" 
   112→FROM "Person" 
   113→WHERE "first_name" NOT LIKE 'H%';
   114→```
   115→
   116→#### IN and NOT IN Operations
   117→
   118→Use IN and NOT IN to check if a column value matches any value in a list:
   119→
   120→```cpp
   121→using namespace sqlgen;
   122→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   123→
   124→// Find people with specific first names (variadic arguments)
   125→const auto query1 = read<std::vector<Person>> | 
   126→                   where("first_name"_c.in("Bart", "Lisa", "Maggie"));
   127→
   128→// Find people NOT with specific first names (variadic arguments)
   129→const auto query2 = read<std::vector<Person>> | 
   130→                   where("first_name"_c.not_in("Homer", "Hugo"));
   131→
   132→// Find people with specific first names (using vector)
   133→const auto names = std::vector<std::string>({"Bart", "Lisa", "Maggie"});
   134→const auto query3 = read<std::vector<Person>> | 
   135→                   where("first_name"_c.in(names));
   136→
   137→// Find people NOT with specific first names (using vector)
   138→const auto excluded_names = std::vector<std::string>({"Homer", "Hugo"});
   139→const auto query4 = read<std::vector<Person>> | 
   140→                   where("first_name"_c.not_in(excluded_names));
   141→```
   142→
   143→This generates SQL like:
   144→
   145→```sql
   146→-- For query1
   147→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age" 
   148→FROM "Person" 
   149→WHERE "first_name" IN ('Bart', 'Lisa', 'Maggie');
   150→
   151→-- For query2
   152→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age" 
   153→FROM "Person" 
   154→WHERE "first_name" NOT IN ('Homer', 'Hugo');
   155→
   156→-- For query3
   157→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age" 
   158→FROM "Person" 
   159→WHERE "first_name" IN ('Bart', 'Lisa', 'Maggie');
   160→
   161→-- For query4
   162→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age" 
   163→FROM "Person" 
   164→WHERE "first_name" NOT IN ('Homer', 'Hugo');
   165→```
   166→
   167→#### Ordering
   168→
   169→Specify column ordering in queries:
   170→
   171→```cpp
   172→using namespace sqlgen;
   173→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   174→
   175→// Order by age ascending
   176→const auto query1 = read<std::vector<Person>> | 
   177→                    order_by("age"_c);
   178→
   179→// Order by age descending
   180→const auto query2 = read<std::vector<Person>> | 
   181→                    order_by("age"_c.desc());
   182→
   183→// Multiple columns with mixed ordering
   184→const auto query3 = read<std::vector<Person>> | 
   185→                    order_by("last_name"_c, "first_name"_c.desc());
   186→```
   187→
   188→This generates SQL like:
   189→
   190→```sql
   191→-- For query1
   192→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age" 
   193→FROM "Person" 
   194→ORDER BY "age";
   195→
   196→-- For query2
   197→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age" 
   198→FROM "Person" 
   199→ORDER BY "age" DESC;
   200→
   201→-- For query3
   202→SELECT "id", "first_name", "last_name", "age" 
   203→FROM "Person" 
   204→ORDER BY "last_name", "first_name" DESC;
   205→```
   206→
   207→#### Updates
   208→
   209→Set column values in UPDATE statements:
   210→
   211→```cpp
   212→using namespace sqlgen;
   213→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   214→
   215→// Update a single column
   216→const auto query1 = update<Person>("age"_c.set(46));
   217→
   218→// Update multiple columns
   219→const auto query2 = update<Person>(
   220→    "first_name"_c.set("last_name"_c),
   221→    "age"_c.set(100)
   222→) | where("first_name"_c == "Hugo");
   223→```
   224→
   225→This generates SQL like:
   226→
   227→```sql
   228→-- For query1
   229→UPDATE "Person" SET "age" = 46;
   230→
   231→-- For query2
   232→UPDATE "Person" 
   233→SET "first_name" = "last_name", "age" = 100 
   234→WHERE "first_name" = 'Hugo';
   235→```
   236→
   237→## Type Safety
   238→
   239→`sqlgen::col` class provides compile-time type safety:
   240→
   241→- Column names are validated at compile time using string literals
   242→- SQL injection is prevented through proper escaping and parameterization
   243→
   244→## Notes
   245→
   246→- The class supports all standard SQL comparison operators: `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`
   247→- Column names are automatically quoted in generated SQL
   248→- The class is designed to be used with the query builder interface
   249→- All operations are composable and can be chained together
   250→- The class supports both value and column-to-column comparisons
   251→- String literals are automatically converted to the appropriate SQL type
   252→- The class is thread-safe and has no mutable state

1→# `sqlgen::group_by` and Aggregations
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::group_by` interface provides a type-safe way to group and aggregate data in SQL queries. It supports various aggregation functions like `count`, `avg`, `sum`, `min`, `max`, and `count_distinct`.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Aggregations
     8→
     9→Perform aggregations without grouping:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→using namespace sqlgen;
    13→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    14→
    15→struct Children {
    16→    int num_children;
    17→    int num_last_names;
    18→    double avg_age;
    19→    double max_age;
    20→    double min_age;
    21→    double sum_age;
    22→};
    23→
    24→const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
    25→    avg("age"_c).as<"avg_age">(),
    26→    count().as<"num_children">(),
    27→    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),
    28→    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),
    29→    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),
    30→    count_distinct("last_name"_c).as<"num_last_names">()
    31→) | where("age"_c < 18) | to<Children>;
    32→
    33→const auto children = sqlite::connect()
    34→    .and_then(get_children)
    35→    .value();
    36→```
    37→
    38→This generates the following SQL:
    39→
    40→```sql
    41→SELECT 
    42→    AVG("age") as "avg_age",
    43→    COUNT(*) as "num_children",
    44→    MAX("age") as "max_age",
    45→    MIN("age") as "min_age",
    46→    SUM("age") as "sum_age",
    47→    COUNT(DISTINCT "last_name") as "num_last_names"
    48→FROM "Person"
    49→WHERE "age" < 18;
    50→```
    51→
    52→### Group By with Aggregations
    53→
    54→Group data and perform aggregations:
    55→
    56→```cpp
    57→using namespace sqlgen;
    58→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    59→
    60→struct Children {
    61→    std::string last_name;
    62→    int num_children;
    63→    int num_last_names;
    64→    double avg_age;
    65→    double max_age;
    66→    double min_age;
    67→    double sum_age;
    68→};
    69→
    70→const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
    71→    "last_name"_c,
    72→    avg("age"_c).as<"avg_age">(),
    73→    count().as<"num_children">(),
    74→    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),
    75→    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),
    76→    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),
    77→    count_distinct("last_name"_c).as<"num_last_names">()
    78→) | where("age"_c < 18) | group_by("last_name"_c) | to<std::vector<Children>>;
    79→
    80→const auto children = sqlite::connect()
    81→    .and_then(drop<Person> | if_exists)
    82→    .and_then(write(std::ref(people)))
    83→    .and_then(get_children)
    84→    .value();
    85→```
    86→
    87→This generates the following SQL:
    88→
    89→```sql
    90→SELECT 
    91→    "last_name",
    92→    AVG("age") as "avg_age",
    93→    COUNT(*) as "num_children",
    94→    MAX("age") as "max_age",
    95→    MIN("age") as "min_age",
    96→    SUM("age") as "sum_age",
    97→    COUNT(DISTINCT "last_name") as "num_last_names"
    98→FROM "Person"
    99→WHERE "age" < 18
   100→GROUP BY "last_name";
   101→```
   102→
   103→## Available Aggregation Functions
   104→
   105→The following aggregation functions are available:
   106→
   107→- `count()` - Counts all rows
   108→- `count_distinct(col)` - Counts distinct values in a column
   109→- `avg(col)` - Calculates average of a column
   110→- `sum(col)` - Calculates sum of a column
   111→- `max(col)` - Finds maximum value in a column
   112→- `min(col)` - Finds minimum value in a column
   113→
   114→Each aggregation function can be aliased using the `.as<"alias">()` syntax.
   115→
   116→## Aggregating Nullable Values
   117→
   118→When working with nullable columns (e.g., `std::optional<T>`), it's important to understand how aggregations handle null values:
   119→
   120→1. The result of aggregating a nullable column must also be nullable (e.g., `std::optional<double>`)
   121→2. Null values are excluded from aggregation calculations
   122→3. If all values in a group are null, the aggregation result will be null
   123→
   124→### Example with Nullable Values
   125→
   126→```cpp
   127→struct Person {
   128→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id;
   129→    std::string first_name;
   130→    std::string last_name;
   131→    std::optional<double> age;  // Nullable age field
   132→};
   133→
   134→struct Children {
   135→    int num_children;           // Non-nullable count
   136→    int num_last_names;        // Non-nullable count
   137→    std::optional<double> avg_age;  // Nullable aggregation
   138→    std::optional<double> max_age;  // Nullable aggregation
   139→    std::optional<double> min_age;  // Nullable aggregation
   140→    std::optional<double> sum_age;  // Nullable aggregation
   141→};
   142→
   143→const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
   144→    avg("age"_c).as<"avg_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
   145→    count().as<"num_children">(),      // Results in int (non-nullable)
   146→    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
   147→    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
   148→    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
   149→    count_distinct("last_name"_c).as<"num_last_names">()
   150→) | where("age"_c < 18 or "age"_c.is_null()) | to<Children>;
   151→```
   152→
   153→In this example:
   154→- The `age` column is nullable (`std::optional<double>`)
   155→- All aggregations of `age` result in nullable values (`std::optional<double>`)
   156→- The `count()` and `count_distinct()` functions return non-nullable integers
   157→- The `where` clause includes both non-null values less than 18 and null values
   158→- If all values in a group are null, the aggregation results (avg, max, min, sum) will be null
   159→
   160→### Important Notes
   161→
   162→- Always use nullable types (`std::optional<T>`) for aggregated values when the source column is nullable
   163→- Count operations (`count()`, `count_distinct()`) always return non-nullable integers
   164→- Null values are excluded from aggregation calculations (avg, sum, max, min)
   165→- When all values in a group are null, the aggregation result will be null
   166→- The type system will enforce these rules at compile time
   167→
   168→## The `.as` Operator
   169→
   170→The `.as` operator allows you to alias columns and expressions in your SQL queries. This is particularly important when mapping query results to C++ structs, as the field names in your struct must match the aliases used in the query.
   171→
   172→### Usage
   173→
   174→You can use `.as` in several ways:
   175→
   176→```cpp
   177→// Method 1: Using the .as() member function
   178→"field1"_c.as<"field">()
   179→
   180→// Method 2: Using the pipe operator with as
   181→"nullable"_c | as<"nullable_field">
   182→
   183→// Method 3: Using as directly with values
   184→as<"one">(1)
   185→"hello" | as<"hello">
   186→```
   187→
   188→### Important Notes
   189→
   190→- Field names in your result struct must exactly match the aliases used in the query
   191→- Fields are matched by name, not by order
   192→- You can alias any column, expression, or literal value
   193→- The alias must be a string literal (using the `as<"alias">` syntax)
   194→
   195→### Example
   196→
   197→```cpp
   198→struct Result {
   199→    std::string field;           // Matches "field1"_c.as<"field">()
   200→    double avg_field2;           // Matches avg("field2"_c).as<"avg_field2">()
   201→    std::optional<std::string> nullable_field;  // Matches "nullable"_c | as<"nullable_field">
   202→    int one;                     // Matches as<"one">(1)
   203→    std::string hello;           // Matches "hello" | as<"hello">
   204→};
   205→
   206→const auto query = select_from<TestTable>(
   207→    "field1"_c.as<"field">(),
   208→    avg("field2"_c).as<"avg_field2">(),
   209→    "nullable"_c | as<"nullable_field">,
   210→    as<"one">(1),
   211→    "hello" | as<"hello">
   212→) | to<Result>;
   213→```
   214→
   215→In this example, each field in the `Result` struct must have a name that matches one of the aliases used in the query. The order of the fields in the struct doesn't matter, but the names must match exactly.
   216→
   217→## Notes
   218→
   219→- The `group_by` clause must be used before `order_by` or `limit` clauses
   220→- You cannot use `group_by` multiple times in the same query
   221→- Aggregation functions can be used with or without `group_by`
   222→- The result type must match the structure of your select statement. Note that fields are matched by name, not order.
   223→- All aggregations are type-safe and will map to appropriate SQL types
   224→- The `Result<...>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed
   225→

1→# ![C++](https://img.shields.io/badge/c++-%2300599C.svg?style=for-the-badge&logo=c%2B%2B&logoColor=white) sqlgen 
     2→
     3→[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
     4→[![Maintenance](https://img.shields.io/badge/Maintained%3F-yes-green.svg)](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp/graphs/commit-activity)
     5→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/C++-20-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     6→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/gcc-11+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     7→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/clang-14+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     8→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/MSVC-17+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     9→
    10→**📖 Documentation**: [Click here](docs/README.md)
    11→
    12→**sqlgen** is a modern, type-safe ORM and SQL query generator for C++20, inspired by Python's [SQLAlchemy](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy)/[SQLModel](https://github.com/fastapi/sqlmodel) and Rust's [Diesel](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel). It provides a fluent, composable interface for database operations with compile-time type checking and SQL injection protection.
    13→
    14→sqlgen is based on and tightly integrated with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp), a C++-20 library for fast serialization, deserialization and validation using reflection, similar to pydantic in Python, serde in Rust, encoding in Go or aeson in Haskell.
    15→
    16→Together, reflect-cpp and sqlgen enable reliable and efficient ETL pipelines.
    17→
    18→## Features
    19→
    20→- 🔒 **Type Safety**: Compile-time validation of table schemas and queries
    21→- 🛡️ **SQL Injection Protection**: Built-in input validation and parameterized queries
    22→- 🔄 **Composable Queries**: Fluent interface for building complex queries
    23→- 🚀 **High Performance**: Efficient batch operations and prepared statements
    24→- 📦 **Modern C++**: Leverages C++20 features for a clean, expressive API
    25→- 🔌 **Multiple Backends**: Support for PostgreSQL and SQLite
    26→- 🔍 **Reflection Integration**: Seamless integration with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp) 
    27→
    28→## Supported databases 
    29→
    30→The following table lists the databases currently supported by sqlgen and the underlying libraries used:
    31→
    32→| Database      | Library                                                                  | Version      | License       | Remarks                                              |
    33→|---------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------|---------------| -----------------------------------------------------|
    34→| MySQL/MariaDB | [libmariadb](https://github.com/mariadb-corporation/mariadb-connector-c) | >= 3.4.5     | LGPL          |                                                      |
    35→| PostgreSQL    | [libpq](https://github.com/postgres/postgres)                            | >= 16.4      | PostgreSQL    | Will work for all libpq-compatible databases         |
    36→| sqlite        | [sqlite](https://sqlite.org/index.html)                                  | >= 3.49.1    | Public Domain |                                                      |
    37→
    38→## Quick Start
    39→
    40→### Installation using vcpkg
    41→
    42→1. Make sure you have the required dependencies installed (skip this step on Windows):
    43→```bash
    44→sudo apt-get install autoconf bison flex # Linux (Ubuntu, Debian, ...)
    45→brew install autoconf bison flex # macOS
    46→```
    47→
    48→2. Set up vcpkg:
    49→```bash
    50→git submodule update --init
    51→./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.sh  # Linux, macOS
    52→./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.bat # Windows
    53→```
    54→
    55→3. Build the library:
    56→```bash
    57→cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_CXX_STANDARD=20 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
    58→cmake --build build -j 4  # gcc, clang
    59→cmake --build build --config Release -j 4  # MSVC
    60→```
    61→
    62→This will build the static library. To build the shared library 
    63→add `-DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON -DVCPKG_TARGET_TRIPLET=...` to the first line.
    64→Run `./vcpkg/vcpkg help triplets` to view all supported triplets. 
    65→Common triplets for shared libraries are `x64-linux-dynamic`, 
    66→`arm64-osx-dynamic` or `x64-osx-dynamic`.   
    67→
    68→Add `-DSQLGEN_MYSQL=ON` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
    69→
    70→4. Include in your CMake project:
    71→```cmake
    72→find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)
    73→target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
    74→```
    75→
    76→### Installation using Conan
    77→
    78→1. Install Conan (assuming you have Python and pipx installed):
    79→
    80→```bash
    81→pipx install conan
    82→conan profile detect
    83→```
    84→
    85→For older versions of pip, you can also use `pip` instead of `pipx`.
    86→
    87→2. Build the library:
    88→
    89→```bash
    90→conan build . --build=missing -s compiler.cppstd=gnu20
    91→```
    92→
    93→This will build the static library. To build the shared library,
    94→add `-o */*:shared=True`. 
    95→
    96→Add `-o sqlgen/*:with_mysql=True` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
    97→
    98→3. Include in your CMake project:
    99→```cmake
   100→find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)
   101→target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
   102→```
   103→
   104→You can call `conan inspect .` to get an overview of the supported options.
   105→
   106→## Usage Examples
   107→
   108→### Hello World
   109→
   110→```cpp
   111→#include <sqlgen/sqlite.hpp>
   112→#include <iostream>
   113→
   114→struct User {
   115→    std::string name;
   116→    int age;
   117→};
   118→
   119→int main() {
   120→    // Connect to SQLite database
   121→    const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("test.db");
   122→    
   123→    // Create and insert a user
   124→    const auto user = User{.name = "John", .age = 30};
   125→    sqlgen::write(conn, user);
   126→    
   127→    // Read all users
   128→    const auto users = sqlgen::read<std::vector<User>>(conn).value();
   129→    
   130→    for (const auto& u : users) {
   131→        std::cout << u.name << " is " << u.age << " years old\n";
   132→    }
   133→}
   134→```
   135→
   136→### Connecting to a Database
   137→
   138→```cpp
   139→#include <sqlgen/postgres.hpp>
   140→
   141→// PostgreSQL connection
   142→const auto credentials = sqlgen::postgres::Credentials{
   143→    .user = "username",
   144→    .password = "password",
   145→    .host = "localhost",
   146→    .dbname = "mydb",
   147→    .port = 5432
   148→};
   149→
   150→const auto conn = sqlgen::postgres::connect(credentials);
   151→
   152→// SQLite connection
   153→const auto sqlite_conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
   154→```
   155→
   156→### Defining Models
   157→
   158→```cpp
   159→struct Person {
   160→    std::string first_name;
   161→    std::string last_name;
   162→    uint32_t age;
   163→    std::optional<std::string> email;  // Nullable field
   164→};
   165→```
   166→
   167→### Inserting Data
   168→
   169→```cpp
   170→const auto people = std::vector<Person>({
   171→    Person{.first_name = "Homer", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 45},
   172→    Person{.first_name = "Marge", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 42}
   173→});
   174→
   175→// Automatically creates table if it doesn't exist
   176→// (recall that the table is fully defined at compile time)
   177→const auto result = sqlgen::write(conn, people);
   178→
   179→if (!result) {
   180→    std::cerr << "Error: " << result.error().what() << std::endl;
   181→}
   182→```
   183→
   184→Or:
   185→
   186→```cpp
   187→...
   188→
   189→// write(...) abstracts these steps away, but
   190→// if you prefer more granular control, you
   191→// can use sqlgen::insert.
   192→const auto result = begin_transaction(conn)
   193→                        .and_then(create_table<Person> | if_not_exists)
   194→                        .and_then(insert(std::ref(people)))
   195→                        .and_then(commit);
   196→
   197→...
   198→```
   199→
   200→Generated SQL:
   201→```sql
   202→BEGIN TRANSACTION;
   203→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Person" (
   204→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
   205→    "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
   206→    "age" INTEGER NOT NULL,
   207→    "email" TEXT
   208→);
   209→
   210→INSERT INTO "Person" ("first_name", "last_name", "age", "email") 
   211→VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?);
   212→COMMIT;
   213→```
   214→
   215→### Querying Data
   216→
   217→```cpp
   218→#include <rfl/json.hpp>
   219→#include <sqlgen/postgres.hpp>
   220→
   221→using namespace sqlgen;
   222→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   223→
   224→// Build a query for adults, ordered by age
   225→const auto query = read<std::vector<Person>> |
   226→                   where("age"_c >= 18) |
   227→                   order_by("age"_c.desc(), "last_name"_c) |
   228→                   limit(10);
   229→
   230→// Execute the query
   231→const auto result = query(conn);
   232→
   233→if (result) {
   234→    // Print results as JSON
   235→    std::cout << rfl::json::write(*result) << std::endl;
   236→} else {
   237→    std::cerr << "Error: " << result.error().what() << std::endl;
   238→}
   239→```
   240→
   241→Generated SQL:
   242→```sql
   243→SELECT "first_name", "last_name", "age", "email"
   244→FROM "Person"
   245→WHERE "age" >= 18
   246→ORDER BY "age" DESC, "last_name"
   247→LIMIT 10;
   248→```
   249→
   250→### Grouping and Aggregating Data
   251→
   252→```cpp
   253→using namespace sqlgen;
   254→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   255→
   256→struct Children {
   257→    std::string last_name;
   258→    int num_children;
   259→    int max_age;
   260→    int min_age;
   261→    int sum_age;
   262→};
   263→
   264→const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
   265→    "last_name"_c,
   266→    count().as<"num_children">(),
   267→    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),
   268→    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),
   269→    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),
   270→) | where("age"_c < 18) | group_by("last_name"_c) | to<std::vector<Children>>;
   271→
   272→const std::vector<Children> children = get_children(conn).value();
   273→```
   274→
   275→Generated SQL:
   276→```sql
   277→SELECT 
   278→    "last_name",
   279→    COUNT(*) as "num_children",
   280→    MAX("age") as "max_age",
   281→    MIN("age") as "min_age",
   282→    SUM("age") as "sum_age"
   283→FROM "Person"
   284→WHERE "age" < 18
   285→GROUP BY "last_name";
   286→```
   287→
   288→### Joining data
   289→
   290→```cpp
   291→using namespace sqlgen;
   292→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   293→
   294→struct ParentAndChild {
   295→    std::string last_name;
   296→    std::string first_name_parent;
   297→    std::string first_name_child;
   298→    double parent_age_at_birth;
   299→};
   300→
   301→const auto get_people =
   302→  select_from<Person, "t1">(
   303→      "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   304→      "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name_parent">,
   305→      "first_name"_t3 | as<"first_name_child">,
   306→      ("age"_t1 - "age"_t3) | as<"parent_age_at_birth">) |
   307→  inner_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2) |
   308→  inner_join<Person, "t3">("id"_t3 == "child_id"_t2) |
   309→  order_by("id"_t1, "id"_t3) | to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   310→```
   311→
   312→Generated SQL:
   313→```sql
   314→SELECT t1."last_name" AS "last_name", 
   315→       t1."first_name" AS "first_name_parent", 
   316→       t3."first_name" AS "first_name_child", 
   317→       t1."age" - t3."age" AS "parent_age_at_birth" 
   318→FROM "Person" t1 
   319→INNER JOIN "Relationship" t2 
   320→ON t1."id" = t2."parent_id" 
   321→INNER JOIN "Person" t3
   322→ON t3."id" = t2."child_id" 
   323→ORDER BY t1."id", t3."id"
   324→```
   325→
   326→### Nested joins
   327→
   328→```cpp
   329→using namespace sqlgen;
   330→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   331→
   332→struct ParentAndChild {
   333→    std::string last_name;
   334→    std::string first_name_parent;
   335→    std::string first_name_child;
   336→    double parent_age_at_birth;
   337→};
   338→
   339→// First, create a subquery
   340→const auto get_children =
   341→  select_from<Relationship, "t1">("parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
   342→                                  "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
   343→                                  "age"_t2 | as<"age">) |
   344→  inner_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
   345→
   346→// Then use it as a source for another query
   347→const auto get_people =
   348→  select_from<Person, "t1">(
   349→      "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   350→      "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name_parent">,
   351→      "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
   352→      ("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"parent_age_at_birth">) |
   353→  inner_join<"t2">(
   354→    get_children, // Use the subquery as the source
   355→    "id"_t1 == "id"_t2) | 
   356→  order_by("id"_t1, "id"_t2) | to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   357→```
   358→
   359→Generated SQL:
   360→```sql
   361→SELECT t1."last_name" AS "last_name", 
   362→    t1."first_name" AS "first_name_parent", 
   363→    t2."first_name" AS "first_name_child", 
   364→    t1."age" - t2."age" AS "parent_age_at_birth" 
   365→FROM "Person" t1 
   366→INNER JOIN (
   367→    SELECT t1."parent_id" AS "id", 
   368→           t2."first_name" AS "first_name", 
   369→           t2."age" AS "age" 
   370→    FROM "Relationship" t1 
   371→    INNER JOIN "Person" t2
   372→    ON t2."id" = t1."child_id"
   373→) t2 
   374→ON t1."id" = t2."id" 
   375→ORDER BY t1."id", t2."id"
   376→```
   377→
   378→Or:
   379→```cpp
   380→using namespace sqlgen;
   381→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   382→
   383→struct ParentAndChild {
   384→    std::string last_name;
   385→    std::string first_name_parent;
   386→    std::string first_name_child;
   387→    double parent_age_at_birth;
   388→};
   389→
   390→// First, create a subquery
   391→const auto get_parents = select_from<Person, "t1">(
   392→    "child_id"_t2 | as<"id">,
   393→    "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name">,
   394→    "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   395→    "age"_t1 | as<"age">
   396→) | inner_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2);
   397→
   398→// Then use it as a source for another query
   399→const auto get_people = select_from<"t1">(
   400→    get_parents,  // Use the subquery as the source
   401→    "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   402→    "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name_parent">,
   403→    "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
   404→    ("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"parent_age_at_birth">) | 
   405→ inner_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t1 == "id"_t2) | 
   406→ order_by("id"_t1, "id"_t2) | to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   407→```
   408→
   409→Generated SQL:
   410→```sql
   411→SELECT t1."last_name" AS "last_name", 
   412→       t1."first_name" AS "first_name_parent", 
   413→       t2."first_name" AS "first_name_child", 
   414→       (t1."age") - (t2."age") AS "parent_age_at_birth" 
   415→FROM (
   416→    SELECT t2."child_id" AS "id", 
   417→           t1."first_name" AS "first_name", 
   418→           t1."last_name" AS "last_name", 
   419→           t1."age" AS "age" 
   420→    FROM "Person" t1 
   421→    INNER JOIN "Relationship" t2
   422→    ON t1."id" = t2."parent_id"
   423→) t1 
   424→INNER JOIN "Person" t2 
   425→ON t1."id" = t2."id"
   426→ORDER BY t1."id", t2."id"
   427→```
   428→
   429→### Type Safety and SQL Injection Protection
   430→
   431→sqlgen provides comprehensive compile-time checks and runtime protection:
   432→
   433→```cpp
   434→// Compile-time error: No such column "color"
   435→const auto query = read<std::vector<Person>> |
   436→                   where("color"_c == "blue");
   437→
   438→// Compile-time error: Cannot compare column "age" to a string 
   439→const auto query = read<std::vector<Person>> |
   440→                   where("age"_c == "Homer");
   441→
   442→// Compile-time error: "age" must be aggregated or included in GROUP BY 
   443→const auto query = select_from<Person>(
   444→    "last_name"_c,
   445→    "age"_c 
   446→) | group_by("last_name"_c);
   447→
   448→// Compile-time error: Cannot add string and int 
   449→const auto query = select_from<Person>(
   450→    "last_name"_c + "age"_c 
   451→);
   452→
   453→// Runtime protection against SQL injection
   454→std::vector<Person> get_people(const auto& conn, 
   455→                              const sqlgen::AlphaNumeric& first_name) {
   456→    using namespace sqlgen;
   457→    return (read<std::vector<Person>> | 
   458→            where("first_name"_c == first_name))(conn).value();
   459→}
   460→
   461→// This will be rejected
   462→get_people(conn, "Homer' OR '1'='1");  // SQL injection attempt
   463→```

1→# `sqlgen::inner_join`, `sqlgen::left_join`, `sqlgen::right_join`, `sqlgen::full_join`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen` library provides a type-safe, composable interface for expressing SQL joins in C++. It supports all standard SQL join types (inner, left, right, full) and allows for both simple and nested join queries, including joining on subqueries.
     4→
     5→## Join Types
     6→
     7→The following join types are available:
     8→
     9→- `inner_join` — Returns rows when there is a match in both tables
    10→- `left_join` — Returns all rows from the left table, and matched rows from the right table
    11→- `right_join` — Returns all rows from the right table, and matched rows from the left table
    12→- `full_join` — Returns all rows when there is a match in one of the tables (not supported by MariaDB)
    13→
    14→Each join type can be used with either a table or a subquery, and can be aliased for use in complex queries.
    15→
    16→## Usage
    17→
    18→### Basic Join Example
    19→
    20→```cpp
    21→using namespace sqlgen;
    22→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    23→
    24→struct Person {
    25→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id;
    26→    std::string first_name;
    27→    std::string last_name;
    28→    double age;
    29→};
    30→
    31→struct Relationship {
    32→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> parent_id;
    33→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> child_id;
    34→};
    35→
    36→// Join two tables: Relationship (as t1) and Person (as t2)
    37→const auto get_children =
    38→    select_from<Relationship, "t1">(
    39→        "parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
    40→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
    41→        "age"_t2 | as<"age">
    42→    ) |
    43→    left_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
    44→```
    45→
    46→This produces a query equivalent to:
    47→
    48→```sql
    49→SELECT t1."parent_id" AS "id", t2."first_name" AS "first_name", t2."age" AS "age"
    50→FROM "Relationship" t1
    51→LEFT JOIN "Person" t2 ON t2."id" = t1."child_id"
    52→```
    53→
    54→### Chaining Multiple Joins
    55→
    56→You can chain multiple joins to build more complex queries:
    57→
    58→```cpp
    59→const auto get_people =
    60→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
    61→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
    62→        "first_name"_t3 | as<"first_name_child">,
    63→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t3) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
    64→    ) |
    65→    inner_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2) |
    66→    left_join<Person, "t3">("id"_t3 == "child_id"_t2) |
    67→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t3) |
    68→    order_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t3) |
    69→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
    70→```
    71→
    72→This produces a query with both an inner and a left join, grouping and ordering the results.
    73→
    74→### Nested Joins and Subqueries
    75→
    76→`sqlgen` allows you to join on subqueries, enabling nested join patterns:
    77→
    78→```cpp
    79→const auto get_children =
    80→    select_from<Relationship, "t1">(
    81→        "parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
    82→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
    83→        "age"_t2 | as<"age">
    84→    ) |
    85→    left_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
    86→
    87→const auto get_people =
    88→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
    89→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
    90→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
    91→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
    92→    ) |
    93→    inner_join<"t2">(get_children, "id"_t1 == "id"_t2) |
    94→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t2) |
    95→    order_by("first_name"_t2) |
    96→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
    97→```
    98→
    99→This produces a query with a subquery in the join clause:
   100→
   101→```sql
   102→SELECT t1."last_name" AS "last_name", t2."first_name" AS "first_name_child", AVG((t1."age") - (t2."age")) AS "avg_parent_age_at_birth"
   103→FROM "Person" t1
   104→INNER JOIN (
   105→    SELECT t1."parent_id" AS "id", t2."first_name" AS "first_name", t2."age" AS "age"
   106→    FROM "Relationship" t1
   107→    INNER JOIN "Person" t2 ON t2."id" = t1."child_id"
   108→) t2 ON t1."id" = t2."id"
   109→GROUP BY t1."last_name", t2."first_name"
   110→ORDER BY t2."first_name"
   111→```
   112→
   113→## Join Syntax
   114→
   115→- `inner_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Inner join with a table
   116→- `left_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Left join with a table
   117→- `right_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Right join with a table
   118→- `full_join<Table, Alias>(condition)` — Full join with a table
   119→- `inner_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Inner join with a subquery
   120→- `left_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Left join with a subquery
   121→- `right_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Right join with a subquery
   122→- `full_join<Alias>(subquery, condition)` — Full join with a subquery
   123→
   124→Where:
   125→- `Table` is the C++ struct representing the table
   126→- `Alias` is a string literal alias for the table or subquery
   127→- `condition` is a boolean expression relating columns from the joined tables
   128→- `subquery` is a previously constructed query expression
   129→
   130→## Aliasing and Column References
   131→
   132→When joining tables or subqueries, you must use aliases to disambiguate columns. Use the `_t1`, `_t2`, etc. 
   133→suffixes to refer to columns from different tables or subqueries, which are defined in the 
   134→namespace `sqlgen::literals`:
   135→
   136→```cpp
   137→"id"_t1, "first_name"_t2, "age"_t3
   138→```
   139→
   140→The library includes predefined suffixes from `_t1` to `_t99`.
   141→
   142→If you want to use your own alias, you can use this syntax instead:
   143→
   144→```cpp
   145→col<"id", "your_alias">, col<"first_name", "your_alias">, col<"age", "your_alias">
   146→```
   147→
   148→## Advanced: Nested and Grouped Joins
   149→
   150→You can nest joins and combine them with grouping and aggregation:
   151→
   152→```cpp
   153→const auto get_people =
   154→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   155→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   156→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
   157→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
   158→    ) |
   159→    inner_join<"t2">(get_children, "id"_t1 == "id"_t2) |
   160→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t2) |
   161→    order_by("first_name"_t2) |
   162→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   163→```
   164→
   165→## Nullability in Joins
   166→
   167→When performing outer joins (`left_join`, `right_join`, `full_join`), columns from the joined table may contain `NULL` values if no matching row is found. `sqlgen` handles this by wrapping the type of such columns in `std::optional`. If a field is already nullable (i.e., `std::optional<T>`), it remains `std::optional<T>`.
   168→
   169→-   `inner_join`: Does not introduce nullability. The types of the selected columns remain unchanged.
   170→-   `left_join`: Columns selected from the right table (the one being joined) will become `std::optional<T>` if they are not already nullable.
   171→-   `right_join`: Columns selected from the left table (the `select_from` table) will become `std::optional<T>` if they are not already nullable.
   172→-   `full_join`: Columns selected from both tables will become `std::optional<T>` if they are not already nullable.
   173→
   174→### Example: Nullability in a `left_join`
   175→
   176→Consider a `left_join` between `Person` and `Relationship` tables. If a person has no corresponding relationship, the columns from `Relationship` will be `NULL`.
   177→
   178→```cpp
   179→struct PersonWithOptionalRelationship {
   180→    uint32_t id;
   181→    std::string first_name;
   182→    std::optional<uint32_t> child_id;
   183→};
   184→
   185→const auto get_people_with_optional_relationship =
   186→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   187→        "id"_t1 | as<"id">,
   188→        "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name">,
   189→        "child_id"_t2 | as<"child_id">
   190→    ) |
   191→    left_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2) |
   192→    to<std::vector<PersonWithOptionalRelationship>>;
   193→```
   194→
   195→In this example, `child_id` is selected from the right table (`Relationship`) of a `left_join`. Therefore, its type in the result struct `PersonWithOptionalRelationship` must be `std::optional<uint32_t>` to handle cases where no matching relationship is found.
   196→
   197→### Nullability in Multi-Table Joins
   198→
   199→Nullability propagates through chained joins. If a table becomes nullable due to an outer join, any subsequent joins that use columns from that table will also treat them as nullable.
   200→
   201→For example, consider a query that joins `Person` to `Relationship` (left join) and then `Relationship` to a hypothetical `Pet` table (left join).
   202→
   203→```cpp
   204→struct PersonWithPets {
   205→    uint32_t person_id;
   206→    std::optional<uint32_t> child_id;
   207→    std::optional<std::string> pet_name;
   208→};
   209→
   210→// Assume Pet table has { id, name, owner_id }
   211→const auto get_people_with_pets =
   212→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   213→        "id"_t1 | as<"person_id">,
   214→        "child_id"_t2 | as<"child_id">,
   215→        "name"_t3 | as<"pet_name">
   216→    ) |
   217→    left_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2) |
   218→    left_join<Pet, "t3">("child_id"_t2 == "owner_id"_t3) | // Joining on a nullable-prone column
   219→    to<std::vector<PersonWithPets>>;
   220→```
   221→
   222→In this query:
   223→1.  The first `left_join` makes columns from `Relationship` (`t2`) nullable. So, `child_id` becomes `std::optional<uint32_t>`.
   224→2.  The second `left_join` joins `Pet` (`t3`). Since `t3` is on the right side of a `left_join`, its columns (like `pet_name`) also become nullable, resulting in `std::optional<std::string>`.
   225→
   226→If an `inner_join` were used for the second join (`Pet`), `pet_name` would still be `std::optional<std::string>` if the `Pet` table itself has a nullable `name` column. However, the join logic itself wouldn't introduce nullability for the `Pet` table's columns. The key principle is that the nullability of a column in the final result depends on both its original type and the types of joins applied to its table.
   227→
   228→## Notes
   229→
   230→- Joins can be chained and nested arbitrarily
   231→- Aliases are required for all joined tables and subqueries
   232→- Join conditions must use the correct aliases for columns
   233→- You can join on subqueries, enabling powerful query composition
   234→- Joins can be combined with `group_by`, `order_by`, and aggregation functions
   235→- The result type must match the structure of your select statement, with field names matching the aliases used in the query
   236→
   237→## Example: Full Nested Join Query
   238→
   239→```cpp
   240→struct ParentAndChild {
   241→    std::string last_name;
   242→    std::string first_name_child;
   243→    double avg_parent_age_at_birth;
   244→};
   245→
   246→const auto get_children =
   247→    select_from<Relationship, "t1">("parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
   248→                                    "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
   249→                                    "age"_t2 | as<"age">) |
   250→    inner_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
   251→
   252→const auto get_people =
   253→    select_from<Person, "t1">(
   254→        "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   255→        "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
   256→        avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
   257→    ) |
   258→    inner_join<"t2">(get_children, "id"_t1 == "id"_t2) |
   259→    group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t2) |
   260→    order_by("first_name"_t2) |
   261→    to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   262→```
   263→
   264→This query joins a table to a subquery, groups by two columns, and computes an aggregate over the join.
   265→

1→# `sqlgen::sqlite`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::sqlite` module provides a type-safe and efficient interface for interacting with SQLite databases. It implements the core database operations through a connection-based API with support for prepared statements, transactions, and efficient data iteration.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Connection
     8→
     9→Create a connection to a SQLite database:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→// Connect to an in-memory database
    13→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect();
    14→
    15→// Connect to a file-based database
    16→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
    17→```
    18→
    19→The connection is wrapped in a `sqlgen::Result<Ref<Connection>>` for error handling:
    20→
    21→```cpp
    22→// Handle connection errors
    23→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
    24→if (!conn) {
    25→    // Handle error...
    26→    return;
    27→}
    28→
    29→using namespace sqlgen;
    30→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    31→
    32→const auto query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>> |
    33→                   where("age"_c < 18 and "first_name"_c != "Hugo");
    34→
    35→// Use the connection
    36→const auto minors = query(conn);
    37→```
    38→
    39→## Notes
    40→
    41→- The module provides a type-safe interface for SQLite operations
    42→- All operations return `sqlgen::Result<T>` for error handling
    43→- Prepared statements are used for efficient query execution
    44→- The iterator interface supports batch processing of results
    45→- SQL generation adapts to SQLite's dialect
    46→- The module supports:
    47→  - In-memory and file-based databases
    48→  - Transactions
    49→  - Prepared statements
    50→  - Efficient batch operations
    51→  - Type-safe SQL generation
    52→  - Error handling through `Result<T>`
    53→  - Resource management through `Ref<T>`

1→# String Operations
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen` library provides a set of string functions for use in queries. These functions are type-safe and map to the appropriate SQL operations for the target database.
     4→
     5→## Motivating Example
     6→Suppose you want to create a report of people with their full names in uppercase, and also want to trim any whitespace from their last names:
     7→
     8→```cpp
     9→struct PersonReport {
    10→  std::string full_name;
    11→  std::string last_name_trimmed;
    12→};
    13→
    14→const auto get_reports =
    15→    select_from<Person>(
    16→        concat(upper("last_name"_c), ", ", "first_name"_c).as<"full_name">(),
    17→        trim("last_name"_c).as<"last_name_trimmed">()
    18→    )
    19→    | to<std::vector<PersonReport>>;
    20→```
    21→
    22→This query produces a list of people with their full names in the format "LASTNAME, Firstname" (with the last name in uppercase) and ensures the last name has no leading or trailing whitespace.
    23→
    24→## String Functions
    25→
    26→### `length`
    27→Returns the length of a string.
    28→
    29→```cpp
    30→length(trim("first_name"_c)) | as<"length_first_name">
    31→```
    32→
    33→### `lower` / `upper`
    34→Converts a string to lowercase or uppercase.
    35→
    36→```cpp
    37→lower("first_name"_c) | as<"first_name_lower">
    38→upper("first_name"_c) | as<"first_name_upper">
    39→```
    40→
    41→### `ltrim`, `rtrim`, `trim`
    42→Removes whitespace (or a specified character) from the left, right, or both sides of a string.
    43→
    44→```cpp
    45→ltrim("first_name"_c) | as<"ltrimmed_name">

1→# ![C++](https://img.shields.io/badge/c++-%2300599C.svg?style=for-the-badge&logo=c%2B%2B&logoColor=white) sqlgen 
     2→
     3→[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
     4→[![Maintenance](https://img.shields.io/badge/Maintained%3F-yes-green.svg)](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp/graphs/commit-activity)
     5→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/C++-20-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     6→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/gcc-11+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     7→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/clang-14+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     8→[![Generic badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/MSVC-17+-blue.svg)](https://shields.io/)
     9→
    10→**📖 Documentation**: [Click here](docs/README.md)
    11→
    12→**sqlgen** is a modern, type-safe ORM and SQL query generator for C++20, inspired by Python's [SQLAlchemy](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy)/[SQLModel](https://github.com/fastapi/sqlmodel) and Rust's [Diesel](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel). It provides a fluent, composable interface for database operations with compile-time type checking and SQL injection protection.
    13→
    14→sqlgen is based on and tightly integrated with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp), a C++-20 library for fast serialization, deserialization and validation using reflection, similar to pydantic in Python, serde in Rust, encoding in Go or aeson in Haskell.
    15→
    16→Together, reflect-cpp and sqlgen enable reliable and efficient ETL pipelines.
    17→
    18→## Features
    19→
    20→- 🔒 **Type Safety**: Compile-time validation of table schemas and queries
    21→- 🛡️ **SQL Injection Protection**: Built-in input validation and parameterized queries
    22→- 🔄 **Composable Queries**: Fluent interface for building complex queries
    23→- 🚀 **High Performance**: Efficient batch operations and prepared statements
    24→- 📦 **Modern C++**: Leverages C++20 features for a clean, expressive API
    25→- 🔌 **Multiple Backends**: Support for PostgreSQL and SQLite
    26→- 🔍 **Reflection Integration**: Seamless integration with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp) 
    27→
    28→## Supported databases 
    29→
    30→The following table lists the databases currently supported by sqlgen and the underlying libraries used:
    31→
    32→| Database      | Library                                                                  | Version      | License       | Remarks                                              |
    33→|---------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------|---------------| -----------------------------------------------------|
    34→| MySQL/MariaDB | [libmariadb](https://github.com/mariadb-corporation/mariadb-connector-c) | >= 3.4.5     | LGPL          |                                                      |
    35→| PostgreSQL    | [libpq](https://github.com/postgres/postgres)                            | >= 16.4      | PostgreSQL    | Will work for all libpq-compatible databases         |
    36→| sqlite        | [sqlite](https://sqlite.org/index.html)                                  | >= 3.49.1    | Public Domain |                                                      |
    37→
    38→## Quick Start
    39→
    40→### Installation using vcpkg
    41→
    42→1. Make sure you have the required dependencies installed (skip this step on Windows):
    43→```bash
    44→sudo apt-get install autoconf bison flex # Linux (Ubuntu, Debian, ...)
    45→brew install autoconf bison flex # macOS
    46→```
    47→
    48→2. Set up vcpkg:
    49→```bash
    50→git submodule update --init
    51→./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.sh  # Linux, macOS
    52→./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.bat # Windows
    53→```
    54→
    55→3. Build the library:
    56→```bash
    57→cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_CXX_STANDARD=20 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
    58→cmake --build build -j 4  # gcc, clang
    59→cmake --build build --config Release -j 4  # MSVC
    60→```
    61→
    62→This will build the static library. To build the shared library 
    63→add `-DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON -DVCPKG_TARGET_TRIPLET=...` to the first line.
    64→Run `./vcpkg/vcpkg help triplets` to view all supported triplets. 
    65→Common triplets for shared libraries are `x64-linux-dynamic`, 
    66→`arm64-osx-dynamic` or `x64-osx-dynamic`.   
    67→
    68→Add `-DSQLGEN_MYSQL=ON` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
    69→
    70→4. Include in your CMake project:
    71→```cmake
    72→find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)
    73→target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
    74→```
    75→
    76→### Installation using Conan
    77→
    78→1. Install Conan (assuming you have Python and pipx installed):
    79→
    80→```bash
    81→pipx install conan
    82→conan profile detect
    83→```
    84→
    85→For older versions of pip, you can also use `pip` instead of `pipx`.
    86→
    87→2. Build the library:
    88→
    89→```bash
    90→conan build . --build=missing -s compiler.cppstd=gnu20
    91→```
    92→
    93→This will build the static library. To build the shared library,
    94→add `-o */*:shared=True`. 
    95→
    96→Add `-o sqlgen/*:with_mysql=True` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
    97→
    98→3. Include in your CMake project:
    99→```cmake
   100→find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)
   101→target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
   102→```
   103→
   104→You can call `conan inspect .` to get an overview of the supported options.
   105→
   106→## Usage Examples
   107→
   108→### Hello World
   109→
   110→```cpp
   111→#include <sqlgen/sqlite.hpp>
   112→#include <iostream>
   113→
   114→struct User {
   115→    std::string name;
   116→    int age;
   117→};
   118→
   119→int main() {
   120→    // Connect to SQLite database
   121→    const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("test.db");
   122→    
   123→    // Create and insert a user
   124→    const auto user = User{.name = "John", .age = 30};
   125→    sqlgen::write(conn, user);
   126→    
   127→    // Read all users
   128→    const auto users = sqlgen::read<std::vector<User>>(conn).value();
   129→    
   130→    for (const auto& u : users) {
   131→        std::cout << u.name << " is " << u.age << " years old\n";
   132→    }
   133→}
   134→```
   135→
   136→### Connecting to a Database
   137→
   138→```cpp
   139→#include <sqlgen/postgres.hpp>
   140→
   141→// PostgreSQL connection
   142→const auto credentials = sqlgen::postgres::Credentials{
   143→    .user = "username",
   144→    .password = "password",
   145→    .host = "localhost",
   146→    .dbname = "mydb",
   147→    .port = 5432
   148→};
   149→
   150→const auto conn = sqlgen::postgres::connect(credentials);
   151→
   152→// SQLite connection
   153→const auto sqlite_conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
   154→```
   155→
   156→### Defining Models
   157→
   158→```cpp
   159→struct Person {
   160→    std::string first_name;
   161→    std::string last_name;
   162→    uint32_t age;
   163→    std::optional<std::string> email;  // Nullable field
   164→};
   165→```
   166→
   167→### Inserting Data
   168→
   169→```cpp
   170→const auto people = std::vector<Person>({
   171→    Person{.first_name = "Homer", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 45},
   172→    Person{.first_name = "Marge", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 42}
   173→});
   174→
   175→// Automatically creates table if it doesn't exist
   176→// (recall that the table is fully defined at compile time)
   177→const auto result = sqlgen::write(conn, people);
   178→
   179→if (!result) {
   180→    std::cerr << "Error: " << result.error().what() << std::endl;
   181→}
   182→```
   183→
   184→Or:
   185→
   186→```cpp
   187→...
   188→
   189→// write(...) abstracts these steps away, but
   190→// if you prefer more granular control, you
   191→// can use sqlgen::insert.
   192→const auto result = begin_transaction(conn)
   193→                        .and_then(create_table<Person> | if_not_exists)
   194→                        .and_then(insert(std::ref(people)))
   195→                        .and_then(commit);
   196→
   197→...
   198→```
   199→
   200→Generated SQL:
   201→```sql
   202→BEGIN TRANSACTION;
   203→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Person" (
   204→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
   205→    "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
   206→    "age" INTEGER NOT NULL,
   207→    "email" TEXT
   208→);
   209→
   210→INSERT INTO "Person" ("first_name", "last_name", "age", "email") 
   211→VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?);
   212→COMMIT;
   213→```
   214→
   215→### Querying Data
   216→
   217→```cpp
   218→#include <rfl/json.hpp>
   219→#include <sqlgen/postgres.hpp>
   220→
   221→using namespace sqlgen;
   222→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   223→
   224→// Build a query for adults, ordered by age
   225→const auto query = read<std::vector<Person>> |
   226→                   where("age"_c >= 18) |
   227→                   order_by("age"_c.desc(), "last_name"_c) |
   228→                   limit(10);
   229→
   230→// Execute the query
   231→const auto result = query(conn);
   232→
   233→if (result) {
   234→    // Print results as JSON
   235→    std::cout << rfl::json::write(*result) << std::endl;
   236→} else {
   237→    std::cerr << "Error: " << result.error().what() << std::endl;
   238→}
   239→```
   240→
   241→Generated SQL:
   242→```sql
   243→SELECT "first_name", "last_name", "age", "email"
   244→FROM "Person"
   245→WHERE "age" >= 18
   246→ORDER BY "age" DESC, "last_name"
   247→LIMIT 10;
   248→```
   249→
   250→### Grouping and Aggregating Data
   251→
   252→```cpp
   253→using namespace sqlgen;
   254→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   255→
   256→struct Children {
   257→    std::string last_name;
   258→    int num_children;
   259→    int max_age;
   260→    int min_age;
   261→    int sum_age;
   262→};
   263→
   264→const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
   265→    "last_name"_c,
   266→    count().as<"num_children">(),
   267→    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),
   268→    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),
   269→    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),
   270→) | where("age"_c < 18) | group_by("last_name"_c) | to<std::vector<Children>>;
   271→
   272→const std::vector<Children> children = get_children(conn).value();
   273→```
   274→
   275→Generated SQL:
   276→```sql
   277→SELECT 
   278→    "last_name",
   279→    COUNT(*) as "num_children",
   280→    MAX("age") as "max_age",
   281→    MIN("age") as "min_age",
   282→    SUM("age") as "sum_age"
   283→FROM "Person"
   284→WHERE "age" < 18
   285→GROUP BY "last_name";
   286→```
   287→
   288→### Joining data
   289→
   290→```cpp
   291→using namespace sqlgen;
   292→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   293→
   294→struct ParentAndChild {
   295→    std::string last_name;
   296→    std::string first_name_parent;
   297→    std::string first_name_child;
   298→    double parent_age_at_birth;
   299→};
   300→
   301→const auto get_people =
   302→  select_from<Person, "t1">(
   303→      "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   304→      "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name_parent">,
   305→      "first_name"_t3 | as<"first_name_child">,
   306→      ("age"_t1 - "age"_t3) | as<"parent_age_at_birth">) |
   307→  inner_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2) |
   308→  inner_join<Person, "t3">("id"_t3 == "child_id"_t2) |
   309→  order_by("id"_t1, "id"_t3) | to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   310→```
   311→
   312→Generated SQL:
   313→```sql
   314→SELECT t1."last_name" AS "last_name", 
   315→       t1."first_name" AS "first_name_parent", 
   316→       t3."first_name" AS "first_name_child", 
   317→       t1."age" - t3."age" AS "parent_age_at_birth" 
   318→FROM "Person" t1 
   319→INNER JOIN "Relationship" t2 
   320→ON t1."id" = t2."parent_id" 
   321→INNER JOIN "Person" t3
   322→ON t3."id" = t2."child_id" 
   323→ORDER BY t1."id", t3."id"
   324→```
   325→
   326→### Nested joins
   327→
   328→```cpp
   329→using namespace sqlgen;
   330→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   331→
   332→struct ParentAndChild {
   333→    std::string last_name;
   334→    std::string first_name_parent;
   335→    std::string first_name_child;
   336→    double parent_age_at_birth;
   337→};
   338→
   339→// First, create a subquery
   340→const auto get_children =
   341→  select_from<Relationship, "t1">("parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
   342→                                  "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
   343→                                  "age"_t2 | as<"age">) |
   344→  inner_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
   345→
   346→// Then use it as a source for another query
   347→const auto get_people =
   348→  select_from<Person, "t1">(
   349→      "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   350→      "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name_parent">,
   351→      "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
   352→      ("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"parent_age_at_birth">) |
   353→  inner_join<"t2">(
   354→    get_children, // Use the subquery as the source
   355→    "id"_t1 == "id"_t2) | 
   356→  order_by("id"_t1, "id"_t2) | to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   357→```
   358→
   359→Generated SQL:
   360→```sql
   361→SELECT t1."last_name" AS "last_name", 
   362→    t1."first_name" AS "first_name_parent", 
   363→    t2."first_name" AS "first_name_child", 
   364→    t1."age" - t2."age" AS "parent_age_at_birth" 
   365→FROM "Person" t1 
   366→INNER JOIN (
   367→    SELECT t1."parent_id" AS "id", 
   368→           t2."first_name" AS "first_name", 
   369→           t2."age" AS "age" 
   370→    FROM "Relationship" t1 
   371→    INNER JOIN "Person" t2
   372→    ON t2."id" = t1."child_id"
   373→) t2 
   374→ON t1."id" = t2."id" 
   375→ORDER BY t1."id", t2."id"
   376→```
   377→
   378→Or:
   379→```cpp
   380→using namespace sqlgen;
   381→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   382→
   383→struct ParentAndChild {
   384→    std::string last_name;
   385→    std::string first_name_parent;
   386→    std::string first_name_child;
   387→    double parent_age_at_birth;
   388→};
   389→
   390→// First, create a subquery
   391→const auto get_parents = select_from<Person, "t1">(
   392→    "child_id"_t2 | as<"id">,
   393→    "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name">,
   394→    "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   395→    "age"_t1 | as<"age">
   396→) | inner_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2);
   397→
   398→// Then use it as a source for another query
   399→const auto get_people = select_from<"t1">(
   400→    get_parents,  // Use the subquery as the source
   401→    "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   402→    "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name_parent">,
   403→    "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
   404→    ("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"parent_age_at_birth">) | 
   405→ inner_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t1 == "id"_t2) | 
   406→ order_by("id"_t1, "id"_t2) | to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   407→```
   408→
   409→Generated SQL:
   410→```sql
   411→SELECT t1."last_name" AS "last_name", 
   412→       t1."first_name" AS "first_name_parent", 
   413→       t2."first_name" AS "first_name_child", 
   414→       (t1."age") - (t2."age") AS "parent_age_at_birth" 
   415→FROM (
   416→    SELECT t2."child_id" AS "id", 
   417→           t1."first_name" AS "first_name", 
   418→           t1."last_name" AS "last_name", 
   419→           t1."age" AS "age" 
   420→    FROM "Person" t1 
   421→    INNER JOIN "Relationship" t2
   422→    ON t1."id" = t2."parent_id"

   428→
   429→### Type Safety and SQL Injection Protection
   430→
   431→sqlgen provides comprehensive compile-time checks and runtime protection:
   432→
   433→```cpp
   434→// Compile-time error: No such column "color"
   435→const auto query = read<std::vector<Person>> |
   436→                   where("color"_c == "blue");
   437→
